summary: The third paper of the series computes Grothendieck-Witt groups of rings. Its structural result, Theorem 1, is that the classical symmetric Grothendieck-Witt spectrum of a ring sits in a fibre sequence with the homotopy fixed points of its K-theory and its symmetric L-theory; the tool is the family of Poincare structures Q^{>=m}_M on the perfect derived category interpolating between quadratic and symmetric forms, and a surgery argument that compares the L-theory of any member of the family with symmetric L-theory in a range depending on how symmetric or quadratic it is. Three consequences are drawn. First, Theorem 7, a localisation-devissage fibre sequence for Grothendieck-Witt theory of a Dedekind ring, which unlike its K-theoretic model needs the symmetric flavour and fails for quadratic forms at the dyadic primes. Second, Theorem 2, a positive solution of Thomason's homotopy limit problem for every Dedekind ring whose fraction field is a number field, 2-adically and integrally exactly when the field is not formally real, which removes the hypothesis that 2 be invertible from the theorem of Berrick, Karoubi, Schlichting and Ostvaer, and proves a conjecture of Berrick and Karoubi. Third, Theorem 4 and its quadratic companions, complete tables of the symmetric, symplectic, quadratic and skew-quadratic Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers, unconditional below degree 20000 and conditional on the Kummer-Vandiver conjecture only as to whether certain odd torsion groups are cyclic; and Corollary 8, that the classical Grothendieck-Witt groups of any number ring are finitely generated. Along the way the symmetric and quadratic L-groups of Dedekind rings are computed in all four residues mod 4, with the correction term at the dyadic primes identified, and the genuine symmetric L-groups are identified with Ranicki's L-groups of short complexes. What the paper needs from outside is Papers I and II of the series for the framework, Hebestreit-Steimle to know that its spectra compute classical forms, Quillen and Weibel for the K-groups of finite fields and of the integers, Milnor-Husemoller and Lam for Witt groups of number rings and of 2-adic fields, and the unpublished Paper IV for multiplicative structures on L-theory.

items.name: Duality on finitely generated projectives, and modules with involution
items.statement: For R a unital associative but not necessarily commutative ring, every duality D on the category Proj(R) of finitely generated projective left R-modules is necessarily of the form D(P) = hom_R(P,M) with M := D(R) an invertible Z-module with involution. An M-valued unimodular symmetric form on P is a self-dual isomorphism φ : P → D(P); with their isomorphisms these form a groupoid Unimod(R;M), symmetric monoidal under orthogonal direct sum.
items.note: The classical starting point; the identification of every duality in this form is stated without proof in the introduction.

items.name: Classical symmetric and quadratic Grothendieck-Witt spectra
items.statement: The classical symmetric Grothendieck-Witt theory of R is the group completion GW^s_cl(R;M) = (Unimod(R;M),⊕)^gp, a group-like E_infinity-space viewed equivalently as a connective spectrum, whose homotopy groups are the higher symmetric Grothendieck-Witt groups GW^s_{cl,*}(R;M). Replacing M-valued symmetric bilinear forms by M-valued quadratic forms gives GW^q_cl(R;M) and the higher quadratic Grothendieck-Witt groups; the even variant GW^ev_cl(R;M) is defined in the same way from even forms.

items.name: Karoubi's splitting after inverting 2
items.statement: After inverting 2 the polarisation map is an equivalence, GW^q_cl(R;M)[1/2] ≃ GW^s_cl(R;M)[1/2], and by work of Karoubi there is a natural splitting GW^s_{cl,*}(R;M)[1/2] ≅ (K_*(R;M)[1/2])^{C_2} ⊕ W_*(R;M)[1/2], where K(R;M) is the K-theory spectrum of R with the C_2-action induced by P ↦ D(P), the first summand is the subgroup of invariants of its homotopy groups with 2 inverted, and the second consists of the Witt groups of symmetric forms and formations, 4-periodic by definition.
items.locator: Introduction, p. 2; quoted from Karoubi, see also [BF85]
items.note: Quoted, not proved here. Theorem 1 of this paper is the integral refinement of this splitting: after inverting 2 its fibre sequence recovers exactly this.

items.name: Theorem 1: the fibre sequence for classical symmetric Grothendieck-Witt theory
items.statement: For every ring R and duality D = hom_R(-,M) on Proj(R) there is a fibre sequence of spectra K(R;M)_{hC_2} --hyp--> GW^s_cl(R;M) --> L^short(R;M), where L^short(R;M) is a canonical connective spectrum whose homotopy groups are Ranicki's original, non-4-periodic, symmetric L-groups. After inverting 2 the sequence recovers Karoubi's splitting, and it also makes the behaviour of Grothendieck-Witt theory at the prime 2 tractable.
items.locator: Introduction, Theorem 1, p. 2; proved as Theorem 1.2.22 combined with the fibre sequence of Paper II
items.note: The first main result. When 2 is a unit in R, Ranicki's L-groups L^short_* are still 4-periodic and isomorphic to the Witt groups, and the sequence is then due to Schlichting. The paper's insight is that it is the NON-periodic classical symmetric L-theory of Ranicki, rather than the 4-periodic L^s used by Ranicki in later work, that makes the statement true for every ring.

items.name: Theorem 2: the homotopy limit problem for Dedekind rings with number-field fraction field
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring whose fraction field is a number field. Then the canonical map GW^s_cl(R;M) → K(R;M)^{hC_2}, induced by sending a symmetric bilinear form to its underlying finitely generated projective module, is a 2-adic equivalence in non-negative degrees.
items.locator: Introduction, Theorem 2, p. 2; proved in section 3.1
items.note: Thomason's homotopy limit problem. The authors say this is, to the best of their knowledge, the first general result on it for a class of rings which are not fields and in which 2 is not assumed to be a unit. The strategy is to use Theorem 1 to reduce to R[1/2], where it holds by Berrick-Karoubi-Schlichting-Ostvaer.

items.name: Theorem 3: quadratic to symmetric comparison for coherent rings of finite global dimension
items.statement: Suppose R is a coherent ring of finite global dimension d. Then the polarisation map GW^q_{cl,n}(R;M) → GW^s_{cl,n}(R;M) is injective for n >= d+2 and an isomorphism for n >= d+3. If moreover R is 2-torsion free and M = R, the map is injective for n >= d and an isomorphism for n >= d+1.
items.locator: Introduction, Theorem 3, p. 3; proved in section 1.3, see Corollary 1.3.10 and Remark 1.3.16
items.note: Coherent means left-coherent and global dimension means left-global dimension, by a stated abuse of terminology; the same result holds on the right, by Remark 1.3.12. Similar statements hold for the Grothendieck-Witt groups attached to any form parameter in the sense of Bak, by Remark 1.3.17.

items.name: Theorem 4: the symmetric and symplectic Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers
items.statement: The symmetric and symplectic Grothendieck-Witt groups of Z are computed in the table of Theorem 3.2.2: explicitly in a range of degrees below 20000, and beyond that conditionally on the Kummer-Vandiver conjecture, in the sense that of some of these groups only the order is determined and the Kummer-Vandiver conjecture implies that those groups are cyclic. The quadratic and skew-quadratic Grothendieck-Witt groups of Z are obtained in Theorems 3.2.9 and 3.2.13, using in addition Theorem 3 and explicit low-dimensional calculations.
items.locator: Introduction, Theorem 4, p. 3; the table is Theorem 3.2.2, with Theorems 3.2.9 and 3.2.13
items.note: A CONDITIONAL result beyond degree 20000: the dependence on the Kummer-Vandiver conjecture is only for cyclicity of certain groups whose order is determined unconditionally. Two dualities on Proj(Z) give the symmetric and the symplectic cases.

items.name: Theorem 5: the genuine symmetric L-groups are Ranicki’s original symmetric L-groups
items.statement: For any ring R and non-negative integer n, the genuine symmetric L-groups L^gs_n(R;M) are canonically isomorphic to Ranicki's original symmetric L-groups; so in the notation of Theorem 1, L^short(R;M) = tau_{>=0} L^gs(R;M). Ranicki's negative symmetric L-groups, defined by him in an ad hoc manner, are also canonically isomorphic to the corresponding negative genuine symmetric L-groups, and are given by L^gs_n(R;M) = L^ev_{n+2}(R;-M) for n = -2,-1 and L^gs_n(R;M) = L^q_n(R;M) for n <= -3, where L^ev and L^q are Ranicki's even and quadratic L-groups.
items.locator: Introduction, Theorem 5 with its addendum, p. 4; proved as Theorem 1.2.22 in section 1.2
items.note: Ranicki's original n-th symmetric L-group has elements represented by Poincare chain complexes of length at most n, for n >= 0. Theorem 5 and the addendum together show that the classical symmetric L-groups are the homotopy groups of the non-connective spectrum L^gs(R;M). Theorem 1 follows from Theorem 5 together with Paper II's fibre sequence.

items.name: Theorem 6: comparison of L-flavours for coherent rings of finite global dimension
items.statement: Suppose R is a coherent ring of finite global dimension d. Then (i) the map L^gs_n(R;M) → L^s_n(R;M) is injective for n >= d-2 and an isomorphism for n >= d-1; and (ii) the map L^gq_n(R;M) → L^gs_n(R;M) is injective for n >= d+2 and an isomorphism for n >= d+3.
items.locator: Introduction, Theorem 6, p. 4; proved in section 1.3
items.note: Part (i) with Theorem 5 improves Ranicki's comparison, which gives injectivity for non-negative n >= 2d-3 and bijectivity for non-negative n >= 2d-2 for Noetherian rings of finite global dimension d. Theorem 3 follows by combining Theorem 1 and Theorem 6. Part (i) also implies that GW^s_cl(R;M) → tau_{>=0} GW^s(R;M) is an equivalence for R a Dedekind domain, which is what lets the paper study the homotopy symmetric theory GW^s instead of the genuine one.

items.name: Theorem 7: the hermitian localisation-devissage fibre sequence
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring, T a multiplicative subset of R, and F_p the residue field R/p at a maximal ideal p of R. Then restriction, localisation, and a choice of uniformiser for every p with p intersecting T non-trivially induce a fibre sequence of spectra (direct sum over the p meeting T) GW^s(F_p; (M/p)[-1]) → GW^s(R;M) → GW^s(R[T^{-1}]; R[T^{-1}] ⊗_R M).
items.locator: Introduction, Theorem 7, pp. 4-5; proved as Corollary 2.2.5, from the devissage Theorem 2.2.4
items.note: The hermitian analogue of Quillen's localisation-devissage fibre sequence. A more general fibre sequence is constructed for localisations of R away from a set of non-empty prime ideals, in a formulation independent of the choice of uniformisers. This establishes a conjecture of Berrick and Karoubi, that Z → Z[1/2] induces an equivalence on the positive 2-localised Grothendieck-Witt groups; the result holds for general rings of integers in number fields, by Proposition 3.1.11.

items.name: Corollary 8: finite generation of the Grothendieck-Witt groups of number rings
items.statement: Let O be a number ring, that is a localisation of the ring of integers in a number field away from finitely many primes, and let epsilon = +1 or -1. Then the classical epsilon-symmetric and epsilon-quadratic Grothendieck-Witt groups GW^s_{cl,n}(O;epsilon) and GW^q_{cl,n}(O;epsilon) are finitely generated.
items.locator: Introduction, Corollary 8, p. 5; proved as Corollary 2.3.19
items.note: Here GW^s_{cl,n}(R;epsilon) abbreviates GW^s_{cl,n}(R;M) for M = R with the involution given by multiplication by epsilon = +/-1. Deduced from Theorem 1 together with a calculation of the symmetric and quadratic L-groups of Dedekind rings. In the quadratic case the result can also be proved by homological stability, but in this generality that argument is not known to carry over to the symmetric case, by Remark 2.3.20.

items.name: Thomason's homotopy limit problem
items.statement: Sending a symmetric bilinear form to its underlying finitely generated projective module gives a canonical map GW^s_cl(R;M) → K(R;M)^{hC_2}. Thomason's homotopy limit problem asks whether this map is a 2-adic equivalence in positive degrees. It has a positive solution for many rings in which 2 is invertible, by work of Hu-Kriz-Ormsby, Bachmann-Hopkins, and Berrick-Karoubi-Schlichting-Ostvaer.
items.locator: Introduction, p. 2; the problem is due to Thomason
items.note: The question Theorem 2 answers for Dedekind rings with number-field fraction field. The cited positive solutions are quoted, not proved here; the Berrick-Karoubi-Schlichting-Ostvaer result for R[1/2] is the input to the proof of Theorem 2.

items.name: Overlap with Schlichting’s announcement
items.statement: Some of the results of this paper were also announced by Schlichting, in work with a published erratum: the calculations of the Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers of Theorem 4 in the symmetric, symplectic and quadratic cases, the localisation-devissage sequence of Theorem 7 in non-negative degrees, and Theorem 3 for the ring R = Z with the trivial involution.
items.locator: Introduction, Remark, p. 5; [Sch19] and its erratum [Sch24]
items.note: Recorded because it fixes what in this paper is independent and what overlaps with an announced result, which matters for attribution in a design job. The paper cites an erratum to that announcement.

items.name: Poincare infinity-category
items.statement: A Poincare infinity-category is a pair (C,Q) consisting of a small stable infinity-category C together with a Poincare structure Q, that is a functor Q : C^op -> Sp which is reduced and 2-excisive in the sense of Goodwillie's functor calculus and whose symmetric cross-effect B : C^op x C^op -> Sp is of the form B(X,Y) = hom_C(X, D(Y)) for some equivalence of categories D : C^op -> C. The functor D is the induced duality, and a Poincare structure is a formal notion of hermitian form on the objects of C.
items.note: Introduced by Lurie as a framework for Ranicki’s L-theory, and developed in Papers I and II of this series. QUOTED, not developed here. Nothing in the atlas owns this notion.

items.name: Poincare objects and the universal properties of GW and L
items.statement: There is a space of Poincare objects Pn(C,Q) consisting of pairs (X,q) with X an object of C and q in Omega^infinity Q(X) such that a certain canonical map X -> D(X) is an equivalence. There are canonical transformations Pn(C,Q) -> Omega^infinity GW(C,Q) and Pn(C,Q) -> Omega^infinity L(C,Q) which exhibit Grothendieck-Witt theory and L-theory as the universal approximation of Pn by a Verdier localising functor, respectively by a bordism invariant additive functor. These universal properties are analogous to that of the map from the groupoid core Cr(C) -> K(C) for a small stable infinity-category.
items.note: QUOTED from Papers I and II; the analogy for K-theory is quoted from Blumberg-Gepner-Tabuada.

items.name: The perfect derived infinity-category of a ring
items.statement: For a ring R, D^p(R) is the perfect derived infinity-category: the infinity-categorical localisation of the category of bounded chain complexes of finitely generated projective left R-modules at the quasi-isomorphisms, equivalently the infinity-category of compact objects of the localisation D(R) of all chain complexes at the quasi-isomorphisms. For a Poincare structure Q on D^p(R) one writes GW(R;Q) := GW(D^p(R),Q).

items.name: Invertible Z-module with involution over a ring (R.1)
items.statement: A Z-module with involution over R is an R (x)^U R-module M together with an R (x)^U R-module map from M^op to M, written m |-> m-bar, such that the double conjugate of m is m, where M^op is M with the action r (x) s . m := s (x) r . m and (x)^U is the underived tensor product over Z. M is invertible if it is finitely generated projective for either of its R-module structures and the map R -> Hom_R(M,M) sending 1 to the involution is an isomorphism, M being regarded as an R-module via the first R-factor in the source and the second in the target.
items.locator: Definition R.1, p. 7; discussed in section [I].4.2, Definitions [I].4.2.2 and [I].4.2.4
items.note: The paper also records the comparison with the more general notion of an invertible H Z-module with involution of Definition [I].3.1.1: restricting along R (x) R -> R (x)^U R, an invertible Z-module with involution gives rise to one of those, and the invertible Z-modules with involution are precisely the invertible H Z-modules with involution which are finitely generated projective rather than merely perfect in either R-module structure. The stronger notion is used because many arguments need the induced duality on D^p(R) to preserve finitely generated projectives, which holds if and only if M itself is finitely generated projective.

items.name: Examples of modules with involution (R.2)
items.statement: (i) When R is commutative, any line bundle L over R gives an invertible Z-module with involution, with M = L and the identity involution. (ii) For a unit epsilon in R, an epsilon-involution on R is a ring isomorphism from R to R^op whose square is conjugation by epsilon and with epsilon-bar = epsilon^{-1}; then M = R with the module structure r (x) s . x = r x s-bar and the involution epsilon times the conjugation is an invertible Z-module with involution over R.

items.name: The Poincare structures Q^{>=m}_M (R.3)
items.statement: For M an invertible Z-module with involution over R and m in Z union {+/- infinity}, the functor Q^{>=m}_M : D^p(R)^op -> Sp is defined as the pullback of hom_R(X, tau_{>=m} H M^{tC_2}) -> hom_R(X, H M^{tC_2}) <- hom_{R (x) R}(X (x) X, M)^{hC_2}, the right vertical map being induced by the m-connective cover and the bottom map by the equivalence hom_{R (x) R}(X (x) X, M)^{tC_2} ≃ hom_R(X, H M^{tC_2}). In the extreme cases one writes Q^q_M := Q^{>=+infinity}_M = hom_{R (x) R}(X (x) X, M)_{hC_2} and Q^s_M := Q^{>=-infinity}_M = hom_{R (x) R}(X (x) X, M)^{hC_2}. These are Poincare structures, all with the same underlying duality D(X) = hom_R(X,M), and the connective cover maps give an infinite sequence of natural transformations Q^q_M -> ... -> Q^{>=m+1}_M -> Q^{>=m}_M -> ... -> Q^s_M, hence analogous sequences of Grothendieck-Witt and L spectra.
items.locator: Definition R.3, p. 8; that these are Poincare structures is Examples [I].3.2.8, and the bottom equivalence is Lemma [I].3.2.5
items.note: The spine of the whole paper: the flavours of Grothendieck-Witt and L-theory it compares are the values of GW and L on this single sequence of Poincare structures.

items.name: When consecutive Poincare structures agree (R.4)
items.statement: Write Hhat^m(C_2;M) = pi_{-m} H M^{tC_2} for the Tate cohomology of C_2 with coefficients in the underlying Z[C_2]-module of M. If Hhat^{-m}(C_2;M) = 0 then tau_{>=m+1} H M^{tC_2} -> tau_{>=m} H M^{tC_2} is an equivalence, hence so is Q^{>=m+1}_M -> Q^{>=m}_M, and it induces equivalences GW(R;Q^{>=m+1}_M) -> GW(R;Q^{>=m}_M) and L(R;Q^{>=m+1}_M) -> L(R;Q^{>=m}_M). Since Hhat^*(C_2;M) is 2-periodic, if this happens for m it happens for every m+2k. In particular if 2 is a unit in R then all the transitions are equivalences; if 2 is not invertible they are not in general, for instance for R = Z.
items.note: This is the precise sense in which the paper’s several flavours of Grothendieck-Witt theory collapse to one when 2 is invertible, and the reason they do not for Z.

items.name: The genuine quadratic, even and symmetric Poincare structures (R.5)
items.statement: Among the Q^{>=m}_M, exactly Q^{>=2}_M, Q^{>=1}_M and Q^{>=0}_M send a finitely generated projective R-module P, regarded as a complex in degree zero, to an abelian group regarded as a discrete spectrum. The values of Q^{>=2}_M and Q^{>=0}_M are the strict coinvariants and the strict invariants of Hom_{R (x)^U R}(P (x)^U P, M) under C_2, canonically isomorphic to the usual abelian groups of M-valued quadratic and symmetric forms on P; and Q^{>=1}_M(P) is the image of the norm, or symmetrisation, map from the first to the second. These three functors are the non-abelian derived functors of those classical form functors, and are called the genuine quadratic, genuine even and genuine symmetric Poincare structures, written Q^gq_M := Q^{>=2}_M, Q^ge_M := Q^{>=1}_M and Q^gs_M := Q^{>=0}_M.
items.locator: Remark R.5, p. 8; the non-abelian derived functor identification is Proposition [I].4.2.22

items.name: The genuine Grothendieck-Witt spectra compute the classical ones (R.5)
items.statement: The connective covers of the Grothendieck-Witt spectra of the three genuine Poincare structures are the group completions of the corresponding spaces of classical forms: tau_{>=0} GW(R;Q^gq_M) ≃ GW^q_cl(R;M), tau_{>=0} GW(R;Q^ge_M) ≃ GW^ev_cl(R;M) and tau_{>=0} GW(R;Q^gs_M) ≃ GW^s_cl(R;M). In particular when M = R(epsilon) comes from an epsilon-involution these are the classical Grothendieck-Witt spaces of epsilon-quadratic, epsilon-even and epsilon-symmetric forms.
items.locator: Remark R.5, p. 9; quoted as the main result of [HS21]
items.note: QUOTED from Hebestreit-Steimle, not proved here. This is the bridge without which none of the paper’s abstract computations would say anything about classical Grothendieck-Witt groups, so a design job must plan or import it explicitly.

items.name: Hermitian and Poincare morphisms
items.statement: A hermitian morphism of Poincare infinity-categories (C,Q) -> (C',Q') consists of an exact functor f : C -> C' together with a natural transformation eta : Q -> f^*Q' = Q' composed with f. It is a Poincare morphism if a canonical induced map f D -> D f is an equivalence. A Poincare morphism is an equivalence of Poincare infinity-categories exactly when f is an equivalence of categories and eta is a natural equivalence.

items.name: Shift periodicity of the Poincare structures (R.6)
items.statement: For every invertible Z-module with involution M over R and every m in Z union {+/- infinity}, the loop functor Omega on D^p(R) extends to an equivalence of Poincare infinity-categories (D^p(R), (Q^{>=m}_M)[2]) -> (D^p(R), Q^{>=m+1}_{-M}), where Q[k] := Sigma^k Q is the k-fold shift and -M is the twist of M by a sign.
items.locator: Proposition R.6, p. 9; quoted from Proposition [I].3.5.3 and Corollary [II].4.3.4, first observed by Lurie for m = +/- infinity
items.note: QUOTED. The engine of every periodicity statement in the paper: it trades a shift of the Poincare structure for a step along the sequence of R.3 together with a sign twist.

items.name: The shifted Grothendieck-Witt spectra GW^{[n]} and symplectic forms (R.7)
items.statement: For R commutative, setting GW^{[n]}(R) = tau_{>=0} GW(D^p(R); (Q^{>=0}_R)[n]) one obtains GW^{[0]}(R) ≃ GW^s_cl(R), GW^{[2]}(R) ≃ GW^{-ev}_cl(R) and GW^{[4]}(R) ≃ GW^q_cl(R). Moreover the symplectic forms, that is the skew-symmetric forms b with b(x,x) = 0 for all x, are precisely the (-1)-even forms: the Tate cohomology Hhat^0(C_2; Hom_{R (x)^U R}(P (x)^U P, R(-1))) is isomorphic to hom_R(P,R_2) with R_2 the 2-torsion of R, the composite of the map from ordinary cohomology sends a skew-symmetric form b to x |-> b(x,x), and the obstruction to lifting b along the norm map is exactly the vanishing of b on the diagonal.
items.locator: Remark R.7, p. 10; the equivalences are obtained from [HS21], and were also announced by Schlichting
items.note: The identification of GW^{[2]} with symplectic forms is what makes Theorem 4’s symplectic column meaningful. The paper notes a direct argument is also possible.

items.name: Metabolic objects and the Bott-Genauer sequence
items.statement: For a Poincare infinity-category (C,Q) one functorially forms Met(C,Q), whose underlying infinity-category is the arrow category of C, with Poincare structure Q^met(f : L -> X) = fib(Q(X) -> Q(L)) and duality (f : L -> X) |-> (D(X/L) -> D(X)); its Poincare objects are the Poincare objects of (C,Q) equipped with a Lagrangian, classically called metabolic forms. The Bott-Genauer sequence is (C,Q[-1]) -> Met(C,Q) -> (C,Q), the functors sending L to the arrow L -> 0 and an arrow f : L -> X to its target. It is both a fibre and a cofibre sequence of Poincare infinity-categories, that is a Poincare-Verdier sequence.
items.locator: Recollection, pp. 9-10; Definition [I].2.3.5, section [I].2.3, Lemma [I].2.3.7, Example [II].1.2.5
items.note: QUOTED from Papers I and II.

items.name: Grothendieck-Witt theory is Verdier localising, and GW(Met) = K
items.statement: Grothendieck-Witt theory is Verdier localising: it sends Poincare-Verdier sequences to fibre sequences of spectra. There is moreover a natural equivalence GW(Met(C,Q)) ≃ K(C). Under this identification the Bott-Genauer sequence induces a fibre sequence of spectra GW(C,Q[-1]) --fgt--> K(C) --hyp--> GW(C,Q), the maps being induced by the projection Pn(C,Q[-1]) -> Cr(C) that forgets the form and by the map Cr(C) -> Pn(C,Q) that sends an object to its hyperbolic form.
items.locator: Recollection, p. 10; one of the main results of Paper II, with Corollary [II].4.3.1
items.note: QUOTED from Paper II.

items.name: Karoubi periodicity in general (R.8)
items.statement: Let U(R,Q) and V(R,Q) denote the fibres of hyp and of fgt respectively. Then for every ring R, every invertible Z-module with involution M over R and every m in Z there is a natural equivalence V(R;Q^{>=m}_M) ≃ Omega U(R;Q^{>=m+1}_{-M}), where -M is M with its involution negated.
items.locator: Theorem R.8, p. 10; quoted from Corollary [II].4.3.4
items.note: QUOTED from Paper II. The general form of Karoubi’s periodicity theorem, valid without assuming 2 invertible. The fibre sequence of item 113 gives V(R;Q) ≃ Omega U(R;Q[2]) since both are Omega GW(R;Q[1]), and combining with R.6 gives the statement.

items.name: Special cases of Karoubi periodicity (R.9)
items.statement: If 2 is a unit in R, Theorem R.8 is due to Karoubi and, all the Q^{>=m}_M being equivalent, takes the form V(R;Q^s_M) ≃ Omega U(R;Q^s_{-M}). There is a second case where it simplifies without 2 being invertible: if R is commutative and 2-torsion free, for instance the ring of integers in a number field, and M = R with the trivial involution, then Hhat^0(C_2;-R) = 0 and Hhat^{-1}(C_2;R) = 0, so Q^ge_{-R} = Q^gs_{-R} and Q^gq_R = Q^ge_R, and periodicity gives V(R;Q^gs_R) ≃ Omega U(R;Q^gs_{-R}), V(R;Q^gs_{-R}) ≃ Omega U(R;Q^gq_R) and V(R;Q^gq_R) ≃ Omega U(R;Q^gq_{-R}).
items.note: The authors add that V(R;Q^gq_{-R}) ≃ Omega U(R;Q^{>=3}_R), and that to the best of their knowledge Q^{>=3}_R cannot be expressed in terms of classical forms - a recorded limit of the classical language.

items.name: Bordism invariance and periodicity of L and of the Tate construction (R.10)
items.statement: For any Verdier localising invariant F of Poincare infinity-categories the Bott-Genauer sequence induces a fibre sequence on applying F; if in addition F(Met(C,Q)) = 0, that is F is bordism invariant, one gets a canonical equivalence F(C,Q[n]) ≃ Sigma^n F(C,Q) for every n in Z. L-theory and the Tate construction K(C,Q)^{tC_2} on K-theory are bordism invariant; for the latter this follows from classical additivity, K(Met(C,Q)) being the induced object, so that its Tate construction vanishes. Consequently, for every ring R, invertible M and m in Z there are natural equivalences L(R;Q^{>=m}_M) ≃ Omega^2 L(R;Q^{>=m+1}_{-M}) and K(R;Q^{>=m}_M)^{tC_2} ≃ Omega^2 K(R;Q^{>=m+1}_{-M})^{tC_2}. In particular L(R;Q^s_M), L(R;Q^q_M) and K(R;M)^{tC_2} are 4-periodic, and 2-periodic if R is an F_2-algebra.
items.locator: Corollary R.10 with the preceding discussion, pp. 10-11; the bordism-invariance criterion is [Lur11] and Proposition [II].3.5.8
items.note: The 4-periodicity of the quadratic and symmetric L-spectra is due to Ranicki and was reworked in this language by Lurie. This corollary is what makes Sigma^4 L^gs ≃ L^gq, used for the quadratic form of Theorem 1.

items.name: Passage to the opposite ring (R.11)
items.statement: For a ring R the association X |-> hom_R(X,R) refines to an equivalence of stable infinity-categories D^p(R)^op -> D^p(R^op). Given a Poincare structure Q on D^p(R), pulling back along its duality and then along this equivalence gives a Poincare structure Q^dual on D^p(R^op), namely the composite of the equivalence with D and then Q. There is then an equivalence of Poincare infinity-categories (D^p(R),Q) ≃ (D^p(R^op),Q^dual), and in particular GW(R^op;Q^dual) ≃ GW(R;Q).
items.note: The device behind the left/right symmetry claimed for Theorem 3 in Remark 1.3.12.

items.name: Notation for the flavours (R.12)
items.statement: The notational conventions fixed for the rest of the paper: the several flavours of Grothendieck-Witt and L spectra of a ring attached to the Poincare structures of R.3, written with the superscripts q, gq, ge, gs and s, and the abbreviation GW(R;Q) for GW(D^p(R),Q).
items.note: Recorded so that the flavour superscripts used throughout the extraction have a definition to point at.

items.name: The fundamental fibre sequence of Paper II
items.statement: For any Poincare infinity-category (C,Q) there is a natural fibre sequence K(C,Q)_{hC_2} -> GW(C,Q) -> L(C,Q), where K(C,Q) is the K-theory spectrum of C with the C_2-action induced by the duality D. This separates K-theoretic from L-theoretic arguments, and specialising it to the genuine symmetric Poincare structure on D^p(R) gives the fibre sequence K(R;M)_{hC_2} -> GW^gs(R;M) -> L^gs(R;M) from which Theorem 1 follows once the genuine symmetric L-groups are identified.
items.locator: Introduction, displayed equation (1), p. 3; quoted from [II].4.4.13
items.note: QUOTED from Paper II, and the single most important import: the whole theme of this paper is to deduce Grothendieck-Witt results from L-theoretic ones through it. Together with Theorem 5 it yields Theorem 1.

items.name: Poincare structures compatible with M, and the two extreme ones
items.statement: A Poincare structure Q on D^p(R) is said to be compatible with M if its underlying duality is D = hom_R(-,M). For such a Q the canonical map Q^q_M -> Q^s_M factors into a pair of natural transformations Q^q_M -> Q -> Q^s_M, exhibiting Q^q_M and Q^s_M respectively as the initial and the final Poincare structure compatible with M.
items.locator: Remark 1.1.1, p. 12; the factorisation is Construction [I].3.2.6 and the extremality Corollary [I].1.3.6
items.note: QUOTED from Paper I. It is what makes the sequence of R.3 a sequence between two extremes.

items.name: r-symmetric and m-quadratic Poincare structures
items.statement: A spectrum E is m-connective if pi_k E = 0 for all k < m, and m-truncated if pi_k E = 0 for all k > m. For r in Z, a Poincare structure Q is r-symmetric if for every finitely generated projective P the fibre of Q(P[0]) -> Q^s_M(P[0]) is (-r)-truncated. Dually, for m in Z, Q is m-quadratic if the cofibre of Q^q_M(P[0]) -> Q(P[0]) is m-connective for every such P.
items.note: The two numerical measures of where a Poincare structure sits between the quadratic and the symmetric extremes; every comparison range in the paper is expressed through them.

items.name: Reduction to P = R and the connectivity shift for r-symmetry and m-quadraticity
items.statement: The fibre of Q -> Q^s_M and the cofibre of Q^q_M -> Q are exact contravariant functors, so the conditions of Definition 1.1.2 need only be checked for P = R. The collection of X for which the fibre is (-r)-truncated is closed under suspensions and extensions; hence if Q is r-symmetric then the fibre of Q(X) -> Q^s_M(X) is (-r-k)-truncated for every k-connective X. Dually the collection of D(X) for which the cofibre is m-connective is closed under suspensions and extensions, so if Q is m-quadratic then the cofibre of Q^q_M(X) -> Q(X) is (m+k)-connective whenever D(X) is k-connective.

items.name: Which of the Q^{>=m}_M are m-quadratic and (2-m)-symmetric
items.statement: The symmetric Poincare structure Q^s_M is r-symmetric for every r and the quadratic one Q^q_M is m-quadratic for every m. More generally, from the fibre sequences tau_{<=m-2} Omega M^{tC_2} -> Q^{>=m}_M(R) -> Q^s_M(R) and Q^q_M(R) -> Q^{>=m}_M(R) -> tau_{>=m} M^{tC_2}, the Poincare structure Q^{>=m}_M is m-quadratic and (2-m)-symmetric. In particular Q^gs_M is 2-symmetric and 0-quadratic, Q^ge_M is 1-symmetric and 1-quadratic, and Q^gq_M is 0-symmetric and 2-quadratic.
items.note: These three numerical facts are what the comparison ranges of Theorems 3 and 6 are computed from.

items.name: The opposite Poincare structure inherits both bounds
items.statement: If Q is an M-compatible r-symmetric and m-quadratic Poincare structure on D^p(R), then Q^dual is an M^dual-compatible r-symmetric and m-quadratic Poincare structure on D^p(R^op). For m-quadraticity it suffices that the cofibre of Q^q_{M^dual}(R^op) -> Q^dual(R^op) be m-connective, and by Remark R.11 that map is Q^q_M(M[0]) -> Q(M[0]), whose cofibre is m-connective because Q is m-quadratic and M is finitely generated projective; r-symmetry is similar.

items.name: Connectivity criterion for representability by a short complex
items.statement: For X in D^p(R) and integers k <= l the following are equivalent: (i) X can be represented by a chain complex 0 -> P_l -> P_{l-1} -> ... -> P_k -> 0 with each P_i a finitely generated projective R-module in homological degree i; (ii) X is k-connective and D(X) is (-l)-connective.
items.note: The technical translation on which the identification of Ranicki's L-groups rests: Ranicki represents classes by Poincare complexes of bounded length, and this lemma turns that into a pair of connectivity bounds, which is the form the surgery arguments use. The proof takes a complex of minimal length and shows it is concentrated in [k,l], using that a surjection of projectives splits.

items.name: The criterion without a duality, and one-sided connectivity
items.statement: Lemma 1.1.6 does not really require a duality: in its absence the statement still holds if D(X) = hom_R(X,R) is treated as an object of D^p(R^op). The same proof also shows that X is k-connective if and only if it can be represented by a chain complex of finitely generated projective modules which is trivial below degree k.

items.name: Free and stably-free refinements of the criterion
items.statement: If M is moreover free as an R-module, the proof of Lemma 1.1.6 shows verbatim that for X in D^f(R) condition (ii) is equivalent to X being representable by a complex as in (i) with each P_i finitely generated stably free. More generally, if Free(R) is contained in a full subcategory C of Proj(R) closed under the duality and under direct sums, and X can be represented by a bounded complex valued in C, then (ii) is equivalent to X being representable by a complex as in (i) with each P_i stably in C, meaning that there are Q_i in C with P_i (+) Q_i in C.

items.name: Poincare pairs, Lagrangians and the metabolic identification
items.statement: The space Pn(C,Q) of Poincare objects consists of pairs (X,q) with q in Omega^infinity Q(X) for which the associated map q^sharp : X -> D(X) is an equivalence. The space Pn_bdry(C,Q) of Poincare pairs consists of triples (f : L -> X, q, eta) with q in Omega^infinity Q(X) and eta a nullhomotopy of f^*(q) for which the induced map eta^sharp : X/L -> D(L) is an equivalence; one then says L is a Lagrangian in X, or a nullcobordism of X. One has Pn_bdry(C,Q) = Pn(Met(C,Q)), and forgetting the Lagrangian is the map induced by the Poincare functor Met(C,Q) -> (C,Q).
items.note: QUOTED from Paper I. For the construction of the L-theory spectra the paper refers to Lurie and to section [II].4.4.

items.name: Cobordism of Poincare objects and the L-groups
items.statement: Two Poincare objects (X,q) and (X',q') are cobordant if (X (+) X', q (+) (-q')) admits a Lagrangian, that is is nullcobordant. The n-th L-group L_n(C,Q) is the group of cobordism classes of Poincare objects for the shifted Poincare structure Q[-n] := Omega^n Q.
items.note: This generators-and-relations presentation of the homotopy groups of the L-spectrum is what the whole of section 1 manipulates; the paper stresses it as the key feature of L-theory it relies on.

items.name: The L-groups are abelian, and agree with the definition of Paper I
items.statement: The cobordism relation is a congruence relation for direct sum, and the diagonal X -> X (+) X is a canonical Lagrangian for (X (+) X, q (+) (-q)), so L_n(C,Q) is an abelian group; the L-groups sit in an exact sequence of monoids pi_0 Pn_bdry(C,Q[-n]) -> pi_0 Pn(C,Q[-n]) -> L_n(C,Q) -> 0. This definition agrees with that of Definition [I].2.3.11, where L_n was the cokernel of the boundary map in commutative monoids: exactness gives a surjection from that cokernel with trivial kernel, and the cokernel is a group by Lemma [I].2.3.10.

items.name: Notation for L-groups and L-spectra of a ring
items.statement: For C = D^p(R) one writes L_n(R;Q) := L_n(D^p(R),Q) and L(R;Q) := L(D^p(R),Q); and when Q is one of the genuine Poincare structures attached to an invertible Z-module with involution M, the notation L^alpha(R;M) of Notation R.12 is used for the corresponding L-groups, alpha ranging over the flavour superscripts.

items.name: The extreme L-theories are the classical quadratic and symmetric ones
items.statement: It is immediate from the definitions that L^q(R;M) and L^s(R;M) are respectively the usual quadratic and symmetric L-theory spectra of R in the sense of Lurie, which also agree with the L-spectra of Ranicki's later work. The intermediate variants are more mysterious, and studying them is the focus of section 1.
items.note: Fixes which of the paper’s flavours are already classical: the two extremes are, the genuine ones in between are not, and Theorem 5 is precisely the identification of the genuine symmetric one with a classical object.

items.name: Surgery data on a Poincare object
items.statement: A hermitian object of the metabolic category is a triple (f : L -> X, q, eta) with q in Omega^infinity Q(X) and eta a nullhomotopy of f^*(q). When (X,q) is Poincare one calls (f,eta) a surgery datum on (X,q). The non-degeneracy condition for the triple to be a Poincare object of the metabolic category is that eta^sharp : X/L -> D(L) be an equivalence, that is that its fibre X' vanish. In general X' need not vanish, but it acquires a canonical Poincare form induced from (f,q,eta).
items.locator: Section 1.1, p. 14, before Proposition 1.1.13; section [II].2.4 for the general discussion
items.note: QUOTED framework from Paper II. Through the eyes of L-theory a Poincare object with a Lagrangian may be replaced by 0, and algebraic surgery is the generalisation of that move to a mere hermitian object of the metabolic category.

items.name: Algebraic surgery preserves the cobordism class
items.statement: Let (X,q) be a Poincare object for Q with surgery datum (f : L -> X, eta). Then the object X' carries a canonical Poincare form q' such that (X,q) and (X',q') are cobordant.
items.note: Ranicki's algebraic surgery in the Poincare infinity-category language. This is the single move by which every representative in an L-group is improved in section 1.2, and hence the engine of Theorem 5.

items.name: The surgery diagram
items.statement: The underlying object of X' and that of the cobordism chi(f) between X and X' are summarised in a surgery diagram consisting of horizontal and vertical fibre sequences, with rows and columns relating L, X, D(L), X/L, chi(f) and X', the maps being D(f) composed with q^sharp and eta^sharp.

items.name: Lagrangian surgery
items.statement: Given a Lagrangian (L -> X, q, eta) for a Poincare object (X,q), equivalently a Poincare object of Met(C,Q), and given a surgery datum for it, that is a commutative square from (Z -> W) to (L -> X) together with a nullhomotopy of the pulled-back form in Q^met(Z -> W), one may perform surgery by Proposition 1.1.13 to obtain a new Poincare object (L' -> X', q', eta') of Met(C,Q). The map W -> X is canonically a surgery datum on (X,q) and (X',q') is the result of surgery with it; in particular if W = 0 then (X',q') is obtained accordingly.

items.name: Poincare objects and allowed Lagrangians of bounded width
items.statement: Let Q be a Poincare structure on D^p(R) compatible with M, and let n,a,b be integers with a,b >= -1, b >= a-1 and n+a even. (i) Pn^a_n(R,Q) is the subspace of Pn(D^p(R),Q[-n]) spanned by the Poincare objects (X,q) with X ((-n-a)/2)-connective. (ii) M^{a,b}_n(R,Q) is the subspace of Pn_bdry(D^p(R),Q[-n]) spanned by the Poincare pairs (L -> X, q, eta) with X ((-n-a)/2)-connective, L ceil((-n-1-b)/2)-connective, and N := fib(L -> X) ≃ Omega^{n+1} D(L) floor((-n-1-b)/2)-connective; such an L is called an allowed Lagrangian for (X,q). Finally L^{a,b}_n(R;Q) is the cokernel, in monoids, of the map pi_0 M^{a,b}_n(R,Q) -> pi_0 Pn^a_n(R,Q) forgetting the Lagrangian.
items.note: The width filtration of the L-groups: the whole of section 1.2 consists in showing that these bounded-width approximations compute the L-groups once a and b are large enough relative to the quadraticity of Q.

items.name: What the width bounds mean in terms of complexes
items.statement: L^{a,b}_n(R;Q) is the monoid of n-dimensional Poincare objects of width a modulo those admitting a Lagrangian of width b. The connectivity assumption in case (i) guarantees, via Lemma 1.1.6 and D(X) ≃ X[n] being ((n-a)/2)-connective, that X is representable by a complex concentrated in [(-n-a)/2, (-n+a)/2], of width a; in particular Pn^{-1}_n(R,Q) is contractible. In case (ii) the assumptions split by parity: if b+n is odd, the conditions on X and N imply the one on L, and both L and N are representable in degrees [(-n-1-b)/2, (-n-1+b)/2], the upper bound for L using D(L) = N[n+1]; if b+n is even then necessarily b >= a, the conditions on X and L imply the one on N, and L is representable in [(-n-b)/2, (-n+b)/2] while N is in [(-n-b)/2 - 1, (-n+b)/2 - 1].
items.note: The paper notes that quadratic surgery in section 1.2 uses only the case b+n odd, whereas symmetric surgery in section 1.3 needs both parities - a bookkeeping point that matters for the two different comparison ranges.

items.name: When the bounded-width L-monoid is already a group
items.statement: If b >= a then the diagonal inside (X,q) (+) (X,-q) is an allowed Lagrangian, so L^{a,b}_n(R;Q) is a group. Under additional hypotheses on Q, Proposition 1.2.6 shows that L^{a,a-1}_n(R;Q) is a group as well.

items.name: Strictly metabolic objects and the Witt group of projectives
items.statement: Let Q be a Poincare structure whose duality preserves Proj(R). A Poincare object (P,q) with P in Proj(R) is strictly metabolic if there is a projective submodule L of P with q restricted to L vanishing in pi_0 Q(L) and with 0 -> L -> P -> D(L) -> 0 exact. The Witt group W(Proj(R);Q) is the quotient of the monoid pi_0 Pn^0_0(R,Q) by the submonoid generated by the strictly metabolic objects; if Q restricts to a functor into abelian groups this is the classical Witt group. There is a canonical isomorphism W(Proj(R);Q) ≅ L^{0,0}_0(R;Q), because a Poincare object (P,q) is strictly metabolic if and only if it admits an allowed Lagrangian - for the non-obvious direction, any nullhomotopy of q restricted to L makes (L -> X, eta) an allowed Lagrangian, since whether the relevant square is cartesian is equivalent to the exactness of the displayed sequence and so independent of the chosen nullhomotopy.
items.note: The bridge from the width filtration to the classical Witt group, which is what makes the degree-zero end of the paper’s computations classical.

items.name: Strictly metabolic 1-quadratic forms are hyperbolic
items.statement: Let P be finitely generated projective and (P,q) a strictly metabolic Poincare object for a 1-quadratic Poincare structure, with strict Lagrangian L -> P, so that the fibre of L -> P is D(L)[-1] and P is isomorphic to L (+) D(L). By the algebraic Thom isomorphism the space of Poincare structures on the object L -> P of the metabolic category is described by the space of shifted forms Omega Q(D(L)[-1]), which is connected because Q is 1-quadratic. Hence (P,q) is equivalent to hyp(L), the hyperbolic form on L. This recovers the classical fact that a strictly metabolic quadratic form on a finitely generated projective module is hyperbolic.
items.locator: Remark 1.2.5, p. 16; the algebraic Thom isomorphism is [I].2.4.6

items.name: Surgery for m-quadratic Poincare structures
items.statement: Let Q be an m-quadratic Poincare structure on D^p(R), fix n in Z and let a,b >= 0 with b >= a-1 and with n+a and n+1+b both even. (i) If a >= n-2m then every Poincare object in (D^p(R),Q[-n]) is cobordant to one which is ((-n-a)/2)-connective. (ii) If b >= n-2m+1 then every Lagrangian L -> X of a ((-n-a)/2)-connective Poincare object is cobordant relative to X to a Lagrangian L' -> X for which both L' and fib(L' -> X) are ((-n-1-b)/2)-connective. In particular, if both inequalities hold then the monoid L^{a,b}_n(R;Q) is a group and the canonical map L^{a,b}_n(R;Q) -> L_n(R;Q) is an isomorphism.
items.note: The central technical result of section 1.2: it says that for a Poincare structure of known quadraticity, bounded-width representatives and bounded-width Lagrangians already compute the full L-group. Every later identification of a genuine L-group with a classical one is an instance of it.

items.name: The width ranges in the surgery proposition
items.statement: In Proposition 1.2.6 the Poincare objects of (i) are concentrated in degrees [(-n-a)/2, (-n+a)/2] and the Lagrangians of (ii) in degrees [(-n-1-b)/2, (-n-1+b)/2].

items.name: Representatives for the quadratic L-groups
items.statement: The quadratic Poincare structure Q^q_M is m-quadratic for every m. For n = 2k even, applying Proposition 1.2.6 with (a,b) = (0,1) shows that every class in L^q_n(R;M) is represented by a Poincare object concentrated in degree -k, and that such an object represents zero if and only if it admits a Lagrangian concentrated in degrees [-k-1,-k]. For n = 2k+1 odd, applying it with (a,b) = (1,0) gives the corresponding statement with the object concentrated in the appropriate two adjacent degrees.
items.note: The classical generators-and-relations description of quadratic L-theory recovered from the general machine; the model for how Theorem 5 will be proved for the genuine symmetric structure.

items.name: Representatives for the genuine symmetric L-groups
items.statement: For any n >= 0, every class in L^gs_n(R;M) can be represented by a Poincare object concentrated in degrees [-n,0], and such an object represents zero if and only if it admits a Lagrangian concentrated in degrees [-n-1,0]. In particular the canonical map L^{n,n+1}_n(R;Q^gs_M) -> L_n(R;Q^gs_M) = L^gs_n(R;M) is an isomorphism for all n >= 0. The proof applies Proposition 1.2.6 with (a,b) = (n,n+1), the genuine symmetric structure being 0-quadratic.
items.note: This is the half of Theorem 5 that matches Ranicki's definition: Ranicki represents an element of the n-th symmetric L-group by a Poincare complex of length at most n, and this corollary produces exactly such representatives, with exactly the corresponding notion of nullcobordism.

items.name: Connectivity of an m-quadratic structure on a shifted projective
items.statement: If Q is an m-quadratic Poincare structure on D^p(R), then for every projective P and every k in Z the spectrum Q(P[k]) is min(-2k, m-k)-connective. The cofibre of Q^q_M(P[k]) -> Q(P[k]) is (m-k)-connective by m-quadraticity, and Q^q_M(P[k]) = (hom_{R (x) R}(P (x) P, M)[-2k])_{hC_2} is (-2k)-connective since P is projective and homotopy orbits preserve connectivity.
items.note: The numerical engine of the proof of Proposition 1.2.6: it is this estimate that makes the restricted form nullhomotopic, so that a surgery datum exists.

items.name: Exactness in the middle for the bounded-width L-groups
items.statement: Under the assumptions of Proposition 1.2.6 the sequence pi_0 M^{a,b}_n(R,Q) -> pi_0 Pn^a_n(R,Q) -> L^{a,b}_n(R;Q) is exact in the middle, as for ordinary L-groups: if a Poincare object of Pn^a_n represents zero in L^{a,b}_n, hence in L_n(R;Q), it admits a Lagrangian, and by part (ii) also one satisfying the connectivity bounds defining an element of pi_0 M^{a,b}_n.

items.name: Quadratic L-theory agrees with an m-quadratic flavour in low degrees
items.statement: If Q is m-quadratic, for instance Q = Q^{>=m}_M, then the natural map L^q_n(R;M) = L_n(R;Q^q_M) -> L_n(R;Q) is an isomorphism for n <= 2m-3 and surjective for n = 2m-2.
items.note: Together with Corollary 1.2.9 this is the comparison that pins the genuine flavours between the two classical extremes. The closing line of the printed proof mistypes the bound as n <= 2n-3; see the source issue.

items.name: The comparison range is essentially optimal
items.statement: The range in which the map of Corollary 1.2.12 is an isomorphism is essentially optimal: for R = Z and m = 0 the map Z/2 ≅ L^q_{-2}(Z) -> L^gs_{-2}(Z) = 0 is not an isomorphism.
items.locator: Remark 1.2.13, p. 18; the two groups are computed in Example 2.3.13
items.note: A concrete counterexample showing the bound cannot be improved, and one of the places where the paper’s own computations for Z feed back into its general theory.

items.name: Widening the Lagrangian bound by one changes nothing
items.statement: For any Poincare structure Q on D^p(R), any n in Z and any a >= 0 with a+n even, the canonical map L^{a,a}_n(R;Q) -> L^{a,a+1}_n(R;Q) is an isomorphism. Surjectivity is clear since both groups are generated by the same Poincare objects; injectivity is proved by splitting off, from a Lagrangian of width a+1, a projective module concentrated in the bottom degree, performing surgery on it in the metabolic category, and observing that the result is the orthogonal sum of the original Poincare object with a term that carries an allowed Lagrangian of width a.
items.note: A purely formal comparison, needing no quadraticity hypothesis, which is what lets the Witt-group end of the theory be reached from the width filtration.

items.name: The Witt group computes L_0 for a 0-quadratic structure
items.statement: Let Q be a 0-quadratic Poincare structure on D^p(R). Then the canonical map W(Proj(R);Q) -> L_0(R;Q) is an isomorphism. Indeed W(Proj(R);Q) ≅ L^{0,0}_0(R;Q) by Remark 1.2.4, and the map factors as L^{0,0}_0 -> L^{0,1}_0 -> L_0, the first being an isomorphism by Proposition 1.2.14 and the second by Proposition 1.2.6.

items.name: The degree-zero L-groups are classical Witt groups
items.statement: (i) L^gs_0(R;M) is naturally isomorphic to the Witt group of M-valued symmetric forms over R. (ii) L^ge_0(R;M) is naturally isomorphic to the Witt group of M-valued even forms over R. (iii) L_0(R;Q^{>=m}_M) is naturally isomorphic to the Witt group of M-valued quadratic forms over R for every m >= 2. For m = 0,1,2 this is Proposition 1.2.15 together with the explicit description of Q^{>=m}_M on a projective module in degree zero; for m > 2 it reduces to m = 2 because L^q_0(R;M) -> L_0(R;Q^{>=m}_M) is an isomorphism by Corollary 1.2.12.

items.name: All even non-positive genuine symmetric L-groups as Witt groups
items.statement: Combining Corollary 1.2.16 with the periodicity equivalences L^gs_{-2k}(R;M((-1)^k)) ≅ L_0(R;Q^{>=k}_M) of Corollary R.10 gives a description of every even non-positive genuine symmetric L-group of R in terms of Witt groups of symmetric, even or quadratic forms, as recorded in Theorem 1.2.22. A similar description holds for the odd L-groups in degrees <= 1, in terms of formations: symmetric in degree 1, even in degree -1, and quadratic in odd degrees <= -3; the paper leaves those details to the reader.
items.note: The odd-degree half is explicitly left to the reader - a recorded gap in the exposition rather than in the mathematics.

items.name: Everything works over finite free complexes, and over intermediate subcategories
items.statement: When M is free as an R-module the results of the section apply verbatim to the full subcategory D^f(R) of finite free complexes: in the proof of Proposition 1.2.6 one may choose P free, so surgery stays within D^f(R), and the connectivity bounds translate into representation by complexes of stably free modules. For instance for Q 0-quadratic every element of L_n(D^f(R),Q) with n >= 0 is represented by a Poincare form on a complex of stably free modules in degrees [-n,0], vanishing precisely when it admits a Lagrangian of stably free modules in degrees [-n-1,0]; and Proposition 1.2.15 holds with stably free in place of projective. More generally one may take any intermediate D^f(R) contained in C contained in D^p(R) closed under the duality, a typical example being the objects whose class in K_0(R) lies in a given involution-closed subgroup.
items.note: The refinement that makes the theory applicable to free and to K_0-constrained variants, which the later sections use when comparing with classical computations.

items.name: Ranicki's n-dimensional Poincare complexes and pairs
items.statement: For n >= 0, an n-dimensional Poincare complex in Ranicki's sense is a pair (C,q) with C an n-dimensional object of Ch^b(Proj(R)) and q an element of H_n(Hom_R(D(C),C)^{hC_2}) whose image in H_n(Hom_R(D(C),C)) = [D(C)[n], C] is an isomorphism D(C)[n] -> C in the homotopy category, where Hom_R is the internal Hom complex and the homotopy fixed points are taken with the standard projective resolution of Z as a trivial C_2-module. An (n+1)-dimensional Poincare pair is a pair (f,eta) with f : C -> C' a map from an n-dimensional to an (n+1)-dimensional complex and eta an element of H_n(fib[Hom_R(D(C),C) -> Hom_R(D(C'),C')]^{hC_2}) whose images in [D(C)[n],C] and [cof(D(C') -> D(C))[n], C'] are isomorphisms in the homotopy category.
items.note: QUOTED from Ranicki; this is the classical object that Theorem 5 identifies with the genuine symmetric L-theory of the paper.

items.name: The short symmetric L-groups
items.statement: Every Poincare pair (C -> C', eta) determines a Poincare complex (C, eta restricted to C), and a Poincare complex arising this way is null-cobordant; two n-dimensional Poincare complexes (C,q) and (C',q') are cobordant if (C (+) C', q (+) -q') is null-cobordant. The set of equivalence classes of n-dimensional Poincare complexes modulo cobordism is an abelian group L^short_n(R;M) under direct sum, the inverse of (C,q) being (C,-q). These are the short symmetric L-groups of R.

items.name: Generality and negative extension of the short L-groups
items.statement: (i) The groups L^short_n(R;M) are formally defined by Ranicki only for M of the form R(epsilon) coming from an epsilon-involution, but the definition uses only the induced duality on chain complexes and so makes sense for any invertible Z-module with involution M. (ii) Ranicki extends the definition to negative integers by L^short_n(R;M) = L^{short,ev}_{n+2}(R;-M) for n = -2,-1 and L^short_n(R;M) = L^q_n(R;M) for n <= -3, where the short even L-groups are the cobordism groups of n-dimensional even complexes: a Poincare complex (C,phi) is even when a Wu class v_0(phi) : H_n(C) -> Hhat^0(C_2;M) vanishes, and an (n+1)-dimensional Poincare pair is even when its relative Wu class vanishes. For n >= 0 the short even L-groups are shown in the proof of Theorem 1.2.22 to agree with the paper's genuine even L-groups.
items.locator: Remark 1.2.20, pp. 20-21; quoted from [Ran80], the even L-groups from its section 3
items.note: The negative extension is what the addendum to Theorem 5 identifies with the negative genuine symmetric L-groups; note that Ranicki defines it in an ad hoc manner, which is why the identification is a theorem and not a definition chase.

items.name: Quasi-isomorphism is finer than cobordism, and the monoid presentation
items.statement: Two Poincare complexes are quasi-isomorphic if there is a quasi-isomorphism f : C -> C' with f^*q' = q; this equivalence relation is finer than cobordism, since a quasi-isomorphism f gives a Poincare pair (id,f) : C -> C (+) C' witnessing the two as cobordant. Hence if Pn^short_n(R) denotes the monoid of quasi-isomorphism classes of n-dimensional Poincare complexes and M^short_n(R) that of n-dimensional Poincare pairs, then L^short_n(R;M) is naturally isomorphic to the cokernel of M^short_n(R) -> Pn^short_n(R) in commutative monoids.
items.note: Puts the classical L-group in exactly the shape of the paper’s bounded-width L-monoids, which is what makes the comparison of Proposition 1.2.23 possible.

items.name: Theorem 5: Ranicki's symmetric L-groups are the genuine symmetric L-groups
items.statement: For every ring R and invertible Z-module with involution M over R, and for all integers n, there is a natural isomorphism L^short_n(R;M) ≅ L^gs_n(R;M) between Ranicki's classical symmetric L-groups and the genuine symmetric L-groups.
items.locator: Theorem 1.2.22, p. 21; announced as Theorem 5 in the introduction
items.note: The main theorem of section 1 and, with the fibre sequence of Paper II, the source of Theorem 1. The proof proceeds in several steps: compare the classical group with the bounded-width L-group of the symmetric structure (Proposition 1.2.23), then show that on n-dimensional complexes a symmetric form is the same as a genuine symmetric form (Lemma 1.2.24), and combine with Corollary 1.2.9. For negative n the even and quadratic identifications of Remark 1.2.20(ii) are used.

items.name: The classical L-group is the bounded-width L-group of the symmetric structure
items.statement: Let I_n be the subcategory of Ch^b(Proj(R)) of n-dimensional complexes and quasi-isomorphisms, and J_{[0,n]} the full sub-infinity-groupoid of D^p(R) spanned by the perfect modules representable in degrees [0,n]. The localisation map restricts to a functor from I_n to J_{[0,n]} and induces natural isomorphisms H_n(Hom_R(D(C),C)^{hC_2}) ≅ pi_n(hom_R(D(C),C)^{hC_2}) ≅ pi_0 Omega^n Q^s_M(D(C)). Sending an n-dimensional Poincare complex (C,q) to the component of (pi(D(C)), rho(q)) is then an isomorphism of monoids Pn^short_n(R) -> pi_0 Pn^n_n(R;Q^s_M), because the functor is an equivalence on homotopy categories and rho is an isomorphism and the localisation preserves direct sums. Consequently, for every n >= 0 this induces a group isomorphism L^short_n(R;M) ≅ L^{n,n+1}_n(R;Q^s_M).
items.note: The proof of the proposition applies the same construction to arrow categories to get the corresponding map on Poincare pairs, compatible with the map on Poincare objects, and notes that every arrow of D^p(R) lifts to a map of chain complexes, which gives surjectivity and hence an isomorphism on quotients.

items.name: Symmetric and genuine symmetric forms agree on complexes of bounded width
items.statement: Let Q be r-symmetric, and let a,b,n be as in Definition 1.2.1 with in addition a <= n+2r-4 and b <= n+2r-3. Then the map L^{a,b}_n(R;Q) -> L^{a,b}_n(R;Q^s_M) is an isomorphism. In particular, since Q^gs_M is 2-symmetric, the map L^{n,n+1}_n(R;Q^gs_M) -> L^{n,n+1}_n(R;Q^s_M) is an isomorphism for every n >= 0.
items.note: The r-symmetric counterpart of Proposition 1.2.6: it is proved by showing that the monoid maps on bounded-width Poincare objects and pairs are already bijections in the stated range. Together with Proposition 1.2.23 and Corollary 1.2.9 it gives Theorem 1.2.22 in non-negative degrees.

items.name: Ranicki's quadratic L-groups, and a warning
items.statement: Ranicki also defines, for n >= 0, the n-th quadratic L-group using quadratic Poincare complexes of dimension n; the same argument as for the symmetric case shows this coincides with L^{n,n+1}_n(R;Q^q_M), hence with L_n(R;Q^q_M) by Proposition 1.2.6. These also agree with the quadratic L-groups of Wall, which arise in manifold theory as the natural recipient of surgery obstructions. The reader is warned that these groups do NOT agree with L_n(R;Q^gq_M), which by periodicity are isomorphic to L_{n-4}(R;Q^gs_M).
items.locator: Remark 1.2.25, p. 23; quoted from [Ran80] and Wall
items.note: An explicitly flagged trap: the paper’s genuine quadratic L-groups are NOT Wall’s quadratic L-groups but a 4-fold shift of the genuine symmetric ones. A design job must not conflate them.

items.name: The setting of connective ring spectra
items.statement: For A a connective ring spectrum, that is a connective E_1-algebra in spectra, with tensor product over the sphere, D^p(R) is replaced by the stable infinity-category Mod^omega_A of compact A-module spectra. A compact A-module is projective if it is a retract of A^n, and Proj(A) is the full subcategory of projective modules. A Poincare structure Q on Mod^omega_A has its duality induced by an invertible module with involution M, assumed projective in either A-module structure so that D preserves Proj(A). As in Definition 1.1.2, Q is m-quadratic if the cofibre of Q^q_M(X) -> Q(X) sends A, equivalently Proj(A), to m-connective spectra; an A-module is k-connective if its underlying spectrum is. With this notion the definition of L^{a,b}_n(A;Q) carries over verbatim.
items.locator: Section 1.2, p. 23; Poincare structures on module categories are treated in section [I].3, with Definition [I].3.1.1

items.name: Surgery for connective ring spectra
items.statement: Suppose Q is m-quadratic on Mod^omega(A). Fix n in Z and let a,b >= 0 with b >= a-1 and n+a, n+1+b both even. (i) If a >= n-2m then any Poincare object in (Mod^omega(A),Q[-n]) is cobordant to one which is ((-n-a)/2)-connective. (ii) If b >= n-2m+1 then any Lagrangian L -> X of such a Poincare object is cobordant relative to X to a Lagrangian L' -> X with both L' and fib(L' -> X) ((-n-1-b)/2)-connective. If both inequalities hold, L^{a,b}_n(A;Q) is a group and L^{a,b}_n(A;Q) -> L_n(A;Q) is an isomorphism.
items.note: The proof is verbatim that of Proposition 1.2.6, once Lemma 1.2.10 is observed to hold in this setting and Lemma 1.1.6 is replaced by Lemma 1.2.27, which is the only place the discreteness of R was used.

items.name: Finite presentation of pi_0 of a compact connective module
items.statement: Let X be a compact connective A-module. Then pi_0 X is finitely presented as a pi_0 A-module; in particular there is a map A^n -> X whose cofibre is 1-connective. The proof reduces to A discrete, since pi_0(A) (x)_A X is connective and perfect over pi_0(A) with the same pi_0, and over a discrete ring connective perfect modules are represented by finite complexes of finitely generated projectives in non-negative degrees.
items.note: The replacement for Lemma 1.1.6 in the spectral setting; it supplies exactly the one consequence of that lemma which the surgery proof needs.

items.name: Recognising projective and length-one modules by connectivity of X and DX
items.statement: (i) If X in Mod^omega(A) is projective then so is D(X), and both are connective; conversely if X and D(X) are both connective then X is projective. The argument takes a fibre sequence A^n -> X -> Y with Y 1-connective, uses that invertibility of M gives hom_A(X,Y) ≃ hom_A(M,Y) (x)_A D(X), concludes that hom_A(X,Y) is 1-connective so the map to Y is nullhomotopic, whence A^n -> X splits and X is a retract. More generally X is a k-fold suspension of a projective if and only if X is k-connective and D(X) is (-k)-connective. (ii) If X is connective and D(X) is (-1)-connective then X need not be projective, but is the cofibre of a map between projective A-module spectra - the analogue of being representable by a complex of projectives in degrees [0,1].
items.note: The spectral analogue of the width bookkeeping of Remark 1.2.2. The printed text cites Lemma 1.1.6 as "Remark 1.1.6"; see the source issues.

items.name: Comparison of L-groups along a 1-connective map of ring spectra
items.statement: Fix m,p in Z. Let f : A -> B be a 1-connective map of connective ring spectra, M and N projective invertible modules with involution over A and B, and Q_M, Q_N Poincare structures on Mod^omega_A and Mod^omega_B which are m-quadratic with respect to M and N. Suppose the extension of scalars f_! refines to a Poincare functor such that the induced map on bilinear parts M -> N is 1-connective and the induced map on linear parts Lambda_{Q_M}(A) -> Lambda_{Q_N}(B) is p-connective. Then L_n(A;Q_M) -> L_n(B;Q_N) is an isomorphism for n <= min(2p-1, 2m) and surjective for n = min(2p, 2m+1).
items.note: The general comparison machine of the subsection: the two connectivity inputs are the bilinear and the linear parts, and the output range is the minimum of what each contributes. Its proof shows first that Q_M(X) -> Q_N(f_! X) is min(2r+1, r+p)-connective when D(X) is r-connective.

items.name: Quadratic to m-quadratic comparison over a ring spectrum
items.statement: Let Q_M be a Poincare structure on Mod^omega(A) which is m-quadratic with respect to a projective invertible module with involution M. Then the canonical map L^q_n(A;M) = L_n(A;Q^q_M) -> L_n(A;Q_M) is an isomorphism for n <= 2m-3 and surjective for n = 2m-2.
items.note: Obtained from Proposition 1.2.29 by taking f the identity and Q_M the quadratic structure; it generalises Corollary 1.2.12 to connective ring spectra.

items.name: L-theory of the sphere spectrum in low degrees
items.statement: Corollary 1.2.30 applies to the universal Poincare structure Q^u on Mod^omega_S, which is 0-quadratic since its linear part is hom(-,S), giving that L^q_n(S) -> L^u_n(S) is an equivalence in degrees <= -3. Moreover, since S^{tC_2} is the 2-completed sphere and hence connective by Lin's theorem, the symmetric Poincare structure Q^s on Mod^omega_S is also 0-quadratic, so L^q_n(S) -> L^s_n(S) is an isomorphism for n <= -3 as well. Both observations also follow from work of Weiss-Williams, who give an explicit formula for the cofibre of the maps in question.
items.locator: Example 1.2.31, pp. 24-25; the universal structure is Example [I].1.2.15, and Lin’s theorem is quoted
items.note: A striking use of Lin’s theorem: it is what makes the symmetric structure on the sphere 0-quadratic, which is false for a general ring.

items.name: Lifting projectives along a pi_0-isomorphism
items.statement: For a map f : A -> B of connective ring spectra inducing an isomorphism on pi_0, in particular for a 1-connective f, the extension of scalars f_! : Proj(A) -> Proj(B) induces an equivalence on homotopy categories. Hence projective B-modules and maps between them lift uniquely up to homotopy to projective A-modules and maps, and consequently perfect B-modules presented as (co)fibres of maps between projectives lift to perfect A-modules of the same kind.
items.note: QUOTED from Lurie; used repeatedly in the proof of Proposition 1.2.29.

items.name: Comparison of L-theories of a ring spectrum with those of its pi_0
items.statement: For A a connective ring spectrum, M a projective invertible module with involution over A, and B a connective E_infinity-ring spectrum: (i) the map L^q(A;M) -> L^q(pi_0 A; pi_0 M) is an equivalence; (ii) the map L^t_n(B) -> L^t_n(pi_0 B) is an isomorphism for n <= 0 and surjective for n = 1; (iii) the map L^gs_n(A;M) -> L^gs_n(pi_0 A; pi_0 M) is an isomorphism for n <= -3 and surjective for n = -2, and if the C_2-action on the spectrum underlying M is trivial it is an isomorphism for n <= -1 and surjective for n = 0.
items.note: All three follow from Proposition 1.2.29 by computing the connectivity of the linear part in each case: trivial for the quadratic structure, 1-connective for the Tate one, and only (-1)-connective for the genuine symmetric one - which is why (iii) has the worse range, improved under a triviality hypothesis on the action.

items.name: The connectivity bound in the genuine symmetric comparison is optimal
items.statement: The invertible module with involution S^{2-2 sigma} (x) ko over ko is an example where the map (S^{2-2 sigma} (x) ko)^{tC_2} -> (pi_0(S^{2-2 sigma} (x) ko))^{tC_2} ≅ Z^{tC_2} is not surjective on pi_0, so that the map on linear parts relevant to Corollary 1.2.33(iii) is indeed only (-1)-connective in general: since pi_*(ko^{tC_2}) is the 2-adic integers with a polynomial generator in degree 4, the source has trivial pi_0 while Z^{tC_2} does not. Another example is S^{2-2 sigma} as an invertible module with involution over the sphere.
items.note: A counterexample showing the range in Corollary 1.2.33(iii) cannot be improved without the triviality hypothesis.

items.name: L-theory of the sphere compared with that of the integers
items.statement: The universal Poincare structure Q^u agrees with the Tate Poincare structure Q^t on Mod^omega_S, so L^u_n(S) -> L^t_n(Z) is an isomorphism for n <= 0 and surjective for n = 1. Considering instead the canonical Poincare functor from (Mod^omega_S, Q^u) to (D^p(Z), Q^gs_Z): both structures are 0-quadratic and the map on linear parts is S -> tau_{>=0} Z^{tC_2}, which is 0-connective, so Proposition 1.2.29 gives that L^u_n(S) -> L^gs_n(Z) is an isomorphism for n <= -1 and a surjection for n = 0.

items.name: Coherent rings and finite global dimension
items.statement: A ring is left-coherent if its finitely presented left modules form an abelian category; the word left is omitted throughout section 1.3, and commutativity of R is not needed there. Noetherian rings are coherent, and valuation rings are a standard example of coherent but not necessarily Noetherian rings. For d >= 0, R has global dimension d if every R-module has a projective resolution of length at most d; when R is coherent such a resolution can be taken with finitely generated modules provided the module is finitely presented.

items.name: The Postnikov t-structure on perfect modules and its interaction with the duality
items.statement: For R coherent of global dimension at most d, the connective cover and truncation functors preserve perfect R-modules, so D^p(R) inherits the Postnikov t-structure from D(R), with D^p(R)_{>=0} the 0-connective and D^p(R)_{<=0} the 0-truncated perfect modules; this uses that the lowest non-trivial homotopy group of a perfect complex is finitely presented. The duality induced by M interacts with it by D(D^p(R)_{>=0}) contained in D^p(R)_{<=0} and D(D^p(R)_{<=0}) contained in D^p(R)_{>=-d}, the first inclusion being immediate from Remark 1.1.7 and the second following from the universal coefficient spectral sequence computing the cohomology of hom_R(X,M), since Ext^i_R vanishes for i >= d+1.
items.note: The hypothesis in exactly the form Proposition 1.3.1 uses it, and the reason finite global dimension enters the symmetric surgery argument at all.

items.name: r-symmetry relative to a t-structure
items.statement: For a stable infinity-category C with a t-structure and a duality D, the Poincare structure Q is r-symmetric if the fibre of Q(X) -> Q^s_D(X) is (-r)-truncated for every X in C_{>=0}, where Q^s_D(X) = hom_C(X,D(X))^{hC_2}. Given integers a,b >= -1 one defines Pn^a_n(C,Q), M^{a,b}_n(C,Q) and L^{a,b}_n(C,Q) as in Definition 1.2.1, the connectivity requirements being read in the given t-structure; for R coherent of finite global dimension these agree with the earlier definitions, and as in Remark 1.2.3 the monoid is a group when b >= a.
items.note: The argument is deliberately cast for a general C with a t-structure, because Theorem 2.2.4 applies it to a category of torsion modules which is not the perfect derived category of a discrete ring.

items.name: Surgery for r-symmetric Poincare structures
items.statement: Let C be a stable infinity-category with a bounded t-structure, and Q an r-symmetric Poincare structure on C with duality D such that D(C_{<=0}) is contained in C_{>=-d} for some d >= 0. Fix n in Z and let a >= d-1, b >= d be integers with b >= a, n+a even and a >= -n+2d-2r. Then (i) every Poincare object in Pn(C,Q[-n]) is cobordant to one which is ((-n-a)/2)-connective, and (ii) every Lagrangian L -> X of such a Poincare object is cobordant relative to X to a Lagrangian L' -> X with L' ceil((-n-1-b)/2)-connective and fib(L' -> X) floor((-n-1-b)/2)-connective. In particular the canonical map L^{a,b}_n(C,Q) -> L_n(C,Q) is an isomorphism.
items.note: The r-symmetric counterpart of Proposition 1.2.6, and harder: symmetric surgery needs the coherence and finite-global-dimension hypotheses, which enter through the t-structure condition on the duality. Parts (i) and (ii) are printed with D^p(R) in place of C; see the source issues.

items.name: Width ranges in the symmetric surgery proposition
items.statement: The Poincare objects of part (i) of Proposition 1.3.1 are concentrated in degrees [(-n-a)/2, (-n+a)/2] and the Lagrangians of part (ii) in degrees [ceil((-n-1-b)/2), ceil((-n-1+b)/2)].

items.name: Symmetric surgery over a coherent ring of finite global dimension
items.statement: Let M be invertible over R with R coherent of global dimension d, and Q an r-symmetric compatible Poincare structure on D^p(R). Then for n >= d-2r: (i) if n+d is even the canonical map L^{d,d}_n(R;Q) -> L_n(R;Q) is an isomorphism; (ii) if n+d is odd the canonical map L^{d-1,d}_n(R;Q) -> L_n(R;Q) is an isomorphism.

items.name: Vanishing and Witt-group description in low global dimension
items.statement: Let M be invertible over R with R coherent of global dimension d, and Q an r-symmetric compatible Poincare structure. Then (i) if d = 0 then L_{2k-1}(R;Q) = 0 whenever k >= 1-r; and (ii) if d <= 1 then L_{2k}(R;Q) is isomorphic to the Witt group W(Proj(R); Omega^{2k} Q(Omega^k -)) whenever k >= 1-r. For Q = Q^{>=m}_M the latter is the classical Witt group of (-1)^k-quadratic forms when k = m-2, of (-1)^k-even forms when k = m-1, and of (-1)^k-symmetric forms for all k >= m.
items.note: Part (i) uses (a,b) = (-1,0) in Proposition 1.3.1; part (ii) uses Corollary 1.3.3 with d = 1 together with Proposition 1.2.14, and the final identification is by inspecting the homotopy of Q^{>=m}_M on a shifted projective.

items.name: Recovering Ranicki's vanishing for semisimple rings
items.statement: A ring has global dimension 0 exactly when it is semisimple, and semisimple rings are Noetherian hence coherent. Part (i) of Corollary 1.3.4 therefore recovers Ranicki's result that the odd-dimensional symmetric and quadratic L-groups of semisimple rings vanish: the symmetric case because Q^s is r-symmetric for every r; the quadratic case by reducing through Corollary R.10 to L^q_{-3}(R;M), which by Corollary 1.2.12 is L^gs_{-3}(R;M), and then applying part (i) with k = -1 since Q^gs is 2-symmetric. For completeness the paper notes that for a field K of characteristic not 2 the group L^q_{4k+2}(K) ≅ L^s_{4k+2}(K) also vanishes: by Corollary 1.3.4 it is the Witt group of anti-symmetric forms over K, and any such form has a symplectic basis, hence a Lagrangian.
items.locator: Remark 1.3.5, p. 28; Ranicki’s result is quoted from [Ran92, Proposition 22.7]

items.name: Exactness in the middle, and strict metabolicity in global dimension zero
items.statement: As in Remark 1.2.11, Proposition 1.3.1 gives that the sequence pi_0 M^{a,b}_n(C,Q) -> pi_0 Pn^a_n(C,Q) -> L^{a,b}_n(C,Q) is exact in the middle whenever a,b,n satisfy its assumptions. In particular for a = b = n = 0 it follows that for every coherent ring R of global dimension 0, every symmetric, even or quadratic M-valued Poincare object in Proj(R) which vanishes in the Witt group is strictly metabolic.

items.name: The Witt group of the heart of a t-structure
items.statement: Let C be stable with a t-structure and a duality D exchanging C_{<=0} and C_{>=0}; then D induces a duality on the heart, making C^heart an abelian category with duality. Let Q^gs be the quadratic functor sending A in the heart to the strict invariants hom(A,D(A))^{C_2}, and let W(C^heart, Q^gs) be the corresponding symmetric Witt group, the quotient of pi_0 Pn(C^heart,Q^gs) by the submonoid of strictly metabolic objects, so that two elements agree in it precisely when they become isomorphic after adding strictly metabolic objects. Since pi_0 Q^s_D(A) = Q^gs(A) for every A in the heart, there is a group isomorphism W(C^heart,Q^gs) ≅ L^{0,0}_0(C,Q^s_D), analogous to Remark 1.2.4.
items.note: The device that turns the L-theory of a t-structured category into a Witt group of its heart; it is applied in Theorem 2.2.4 to torsion modules, which is where devissage comes from.

items.name: Examples of hearts: projectives, and torsion modules
items.statement: If R has global dimension 0 the heart of D^p(R) is Proj(R) and W of the heart is the classical Witt group of symmetric forms of Remark 1.2.4. Another example is given by certain torsion modules over a 1-dimensional ring, which is elaborated and exploited in Theorem 2.2.4.

items.name: Symmetric L-groups of a t-structured category as Witt groups of the heart
items.statement: In the above situation, with Q^s_D the symmetric Poincare structure associated to D, there are canonical isomorphisms L_n(C;Q^s_D) ≅ W(C^heart,Q^gs) for n congruent to 0 mod 4, ≅ W(C^heart,Q^gs_{-D}) for n congruent to 2 mod 4, and 0 otherwise, where -D denotes the duality with the structural isomorphism negated. In particular every element of pi_0 Pn(C^heart,Q^gs) which vanishes in the Witt group is metabolic. The proof applies Proposition 1.3.1 with r infinite and d = 0, taking (a,b) = (0,0) for n even and (-1,0) for n odd.
items.note: The 4-periodic Witt-theoretic computation of symmetric L-theory in global dimension zero, and the engine of the devissage theorem of section 2.2.

items.name: Comparison of an r-symmetric flavour with symmetric L-theory
items.statement: Let M be invertible over R with R coherent of global dimension d, and Q an r-symmetric compatible Poincare structure on D^p(R). Then the canonical map L_n(R;Q) -> L_n(R;Q^s_M) = L^s_n(R;M) is injective for n >= d-2r+2 and bijective for n >= d-2r+3.
items.note: The r-symmetric analogue of Corollary 1.2.12, and the immediate source of Theorem 6. The injectivity at the bottom of the range is proved by showing that a Lagrangian for the symmetric structure with the right connectivity refines to one for Q, using that the comparison map on Q of a sufficiently connective L is (-1)-truncated.

items.name: Theorem 6: comparison of the genuine flavours with the symmetric one
items.statement: Let M be invertible over R with R coherent of finite global dimension d. Then the canonical maps L^gs_n(R;M) -> L^s_n(R;M) and GW^gs_n(R;M) -> GW^s_n(R;M) are injective for n >= d-2 and bijective for n >= d-1; and the maps L^gq_n(R;M) -> L^s_n(R;M) and GW^gq_n(R;M) -> GW^s_n(R;M) are injective for n >= d+2 and bijective for n >= d+3.
items.locator: Corollary 1.3.10, pp. 30-31; this proves Theorem 6 and the first part of Theorem 3
items.note: The Grothendieck-Witt half follows from the L-theory half because, by Theorem 1, the squares relating GW and L for the quadratic, genuine symmetric and symmetric structures are pullbacks; the L-theory half is Corollary 1.3.9 with the numerical facts that Q^gs is 2-symmetric and Q^gq is 0-symmetric.

items.name: Sharpness of the comparison bounds
items.statement: The bounds of Corollary 1.3.10 are in general sharp. For the d-dimensional ring F_2[Z^d] with the anti-involution induced by inversion of the group, the map L^gs -> L^s is not surjective on pi_{d-2}: by the Ranicki-Shaneson splitting - proved by Ranicki for L^s and by Milgram-Ranicki for L^gs, and reproved uniformly in Paper IV - one has L(R[Z];Q) ≃ L(R;Q) (+) Sigma L(R;Q) for Q = Q^gs, Q^s whenever K_0(R) ≅ K_0(R[Z]) ≅ Z, so by induction the map for F_2 is a retract of the map for F_2[Z^d], and L^s_2(F_2) ≅ Z/2 while L^gs(F_2) = 0.
