A similar argument shows that for epsilon = -1 the map L^gs_0(Z[Z];epsilon) -> L^s_0(Z[Z];epsilon) is not surjective on pi_0; for d = 0 this shows sharpness also for commutative rings with trivial anti-involution. Moreover the map L^gs(Z/4) -> L^s(Z/4) is not an isomorphism on almost all positive homotopy groups. On the other hand Schlichting has shown that L^gs(R) -> L^s(R) is an isomorphism on pi_n for n >= -1 for many regular Noetherian domains of arbitrary finite Krull dimension, so among regular Noetherian rings the bounds are far from optimal.
items.locator: Example 1.3.11, pp. 31; the Z/4 statement is quoted from [Rea24, Corollary F] and the regular-Noetherian statement from [Sch25]
items.note: Records both the sharpness examples and the explicit statement that for regular Noetherian rings the paper’s bounds are not optimal - important for a design job, which should not plan the bounds as best possible.

items.name: The right-handed versions
items.statement: If R is right-coherent of finite right-global dimension, the conclusions of Corollaries 1.3.4, 1.3.9 and 1.3.10 and of Remark 1.3.5 hold for R as well: apply them to R^op with the Poincare structure Q^dual of Remark R.11, which is r-symmetric when Q is by Example 1.1.5, and transport along the equivalence of Poincare infinity-categories (D^p(R^op),Q^dual) ≃ (D^p(R),Q).
items.note: This is the justification of the left/right abuse of terminology announced for Theorem 3 in the introduction.

items.name: Improvement on Ranicki's comparison range
items.statement: Since Theorem 1.2.22 identifies the non-negative genuine symmetric L-groups with Ranicki's L-groups of short complexes, the range of Corollary 1.3.10 improves Ranicki's classical theorem, which gave injectivity of L^gs_n(R) -> L^s_n(R) for non-negative n >= 2d-3 and bijectivity for non-negative n >= 2d-2 for Noetherian rings of global dimension d.

items.name: The Dedekind case, and 4-periodicity in non-negative degrees
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring, for instance the ring of integers in a number field; Dedekind rings have global dimension at most 1. Then the canonical maps L^gs_n(R;M) -> L^s_n(R;M) and GW^gs_n(R;M) -> GW^s_n(R;M) are injective for n = -1 and bijective for n >= 0; in particular the non-negative homotopy groups of L^gs(R;M) are 4-periodic. Similarly the maps L^gq_n(R;M) -> L^s_n(R;M) and GW^gq_n(R;M) -> GW^s_n(R;M) are injective for n = 3 and bijective for n >= 4. By the main theorem of [HS21] the non-negative homotopy groups of GW^gs and GW^gq are the classical Grothendieck-Witt groups of symmetric and quadratic forms.
items.note: The case the rest of the paper works in: it is what allows sections 2 and 3 to study the homotopy symmetric theory GW^s rather than the genuine one.

items.name: Classical Grothendieck-Witt theory of a Dedekind ring is the homotopy symmetric one
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring and M an invertible Z-module with involution over R. Then the canonical maps GW^s_cl(R;M) -> tau_{>=0} GW^s(R;M) and tau_{>=4} GW^q_cl(R;M) -> tau_{>=4} GW^s(R;M) are equivalences.
items.note: The precise statement that licenses the paper’s strategy of computing with GW^s: for Dedekind rings the classical object is exactly its connective cover.

items.name: The 2-torsion-free improvement, and the second half of Theorem 3
items.statement: Let R be coherent of finite global dimension d. There are equivalences Sigma^2 L^gs(R) ≃ L^{-ge}(R) and Sigma^2 L^ge(R) ≃ L^{-gq}(R). If R is in addition 2-torsion free - for instance a Dedekind domain whose fraction field has characteristic different from 2 - then the canonical maps Q^{-ge} -> Q^{-gs} and Q^gq -> Q^ge are equivalences by Remark R.4, so there are canonical equivalences Sigma^2 L^gs(R) ≃ L^{-gs}(R) and Sigma^2 L^gq(R) ≃ L^{-gq}(R). The comparison map is compatible with these, so L^gq(R) -> L^gs(R) is a 2-fold loop of L^{-gq}(R) -> L^{-gs}(R), and Corollary 1.3.10 then gives that L^gq_n(R) -> L^gs_n(R) and GW^q_{cl,n}(R) -> GW^s_{cl,n}(R) are injective for n = d and isomorphisms for n >= d+1.
items.locator: Remark 1.3.16, p. 32; this proves the second part of Theorem 3
items.note: The 2-torsion-free hypothesis buys two degrees, which is exactly the improvement stated in the second sentence of Theorem 3.

items.name: Form parameters in the sense of Bak, and their comparison ranges
items.statement: To any form parameter lambda on an invertible Z-module with involution M there is an associated non-abelian derived Poincare structure Q^{g lambda}_M. Since Q^{g lambda}_M(P[0]) is discrete by definition, it is 0-quadratic and 0-symmetric, so the comparison results of Corollary 1.2.12 and Corollary 1.3.9 apply to it. Depending on lambda it may in fact be 1-symmetric, as for even forms, or 2-symmetric, as for symmetric forms, and likewise 1-quadratic or 2-quadratic. Hence for a form parameter lambda = (M,Q) over a 1-dimensional ring R the map L^{g lambda}_n(R) -> L^s_n(R) is injective for n = 3 and bijective for n >= 4; and L^{g lambda}_2(R) is isomorphic to the Witt group associated to the form parameter (-M, ker(M -> Q)), by Corollary 1.3.4.
items.locator: Remark 1.3.17, p. 32; the notion is Definition [I].4.2.26, after Baues and Schlichting extending Bak
items.note: This is the generality in which the introduction says Theorem 3 also holds - for any form parameter in the sense of Bak in place of quadratic forms.

items.name: The Burnside-ring form parameter and its L-theory
items.statement: The Poincare structure Q^b on D^p(Z) is defined as the pullback of Q^gs(X) -> hom_Z(X, tau_{>=0} Z^{tC_2}) <- hom_Z(X, tau_{>=1/2} Z^{tC_2}), where tau_{>=1/2} Z^{tC_2} is the fibre product of Z and tau_{>=0} Z^{tC_2} over Z/2. It is the Poincare structure of the Burnside ring form parameter, with Q the fibre product of Z with Z over Z/2, M = Z, and M -> Q the pair (2,0). Since M -> Q is injective, Remark 1.3.17 gives that L^b_n(Z) -> L^s_n(Z) is an isomorphism for n >= 2, using L^s_3(Z) = 0. Applying Proposition 1.2.29 to the canonical Poincare functor from (Mod^omega_S, Q^u) to (D^p(Z), Q^b), whose map on linear terms is S -> tau_{>=1/2} Z^{tC_2} and is 1-connective, gives that L^u_n(S) -> L^b_n(Z) is an isomorphism for n <= 0 and a surjection for n = 1.
items.locator: Example 1.3.18, pp. 32-33; the L-theory L^b(Z) was first investigated in [DO19]
items.note: A worked example tying the paper’s machinery to the L-theory studied by Dotto-Ogle; it is also where the sphere and the integers are compared most sharply.

items.name: Dedekind rings and the goal of section 2
items.statement: Dedekind rings are commutative regular Noetherian domains of global dimension 1; the main examples of interest are those whose fraction field is a number field, and other notable ones are discrete valuation rings and rings of functions of smooth affine curves over fields. The goal of section 2 is to extend Quillen's localisation-devissage sequence for Dedekind rings to hermitian K-theory, proving Theorem 7. The route is to construct a Poincare-Verdier sequence from the map of a Dedekind ring to its localisation away from a set S of non-zero primes, use that GW takes such sequences to fibre sequences, and identify the fibre term by devissage as the sum of the GW-spectra of the residue fields.
items.note: Prior art as the paper lists it: three- and four-term localisation sequences for Witt groups in Knebusch and Milnor-Husemoller, extended to long exact sequences of L-groups by Ranicki and to Balmer-Witt groups by Balmer; and for Grothendieck-Witt groups, exact sequences due to Karoubi and to Hornbostel-Schlichting, both assuming 2 invertible. The paper's results need no such assumption, for the homotopy theoretic GW^s.

items.name: Localisation away from a set of primes, and the torsion subcategory
items.statement: For R Dedekind and S a set of non-zero primes, R_S = O(U) where O is the structure sheaf of spec(R) and U is the complement of S, defined as a colimit over open subsets containing U when S is infinite. Concretely R_S is the subring of the fraction field K of elements x with nu_p(x) >= 0 for every p not in S, that is the localisation of R away from S. D^p_S(R) denotes the fibre of D^p(R) -> D^p(R_S), which is the full subcategory of perfect R-modules whose homotopy groups are S-primary torsion, also called S-infinity-torsion modules.

items.name: Examples of these localisations
items.statement: (i) If S is all the non-zero primes then R_S is the fraction field K. (ii) For a multiplicative subset T of R, taking S to be the primes meeting T gives R_S = R[T^{-1}]. (iii) If S is finite and a product of powers of its primes is a principal ideal (x) then R_S = R[1/x]. The reader is warned that in general R_S is NOT obtained from R by inverting a multiplicative subset.
items.note: Case (ii) is what turns the general localisation sequence into the form stated as Theorem 7 in the introduction.

items.name: The localisation is a derived localisation with perfectly generated fibre
items.statement: A map of rings is a derived localisation if the map from the derived tensor product B (x)_A B -> B is an equivalence, equivalently for B flat over A that the underived multiplication map is an isomorphism; it has perfectly generated fibre if the fibre of A -> B is a filtered colimit of perfect B-torsion complexes. For R Dedekind and S a set of non-zero primes, R_S is flat over R and R -> R_S is a derived localisation with perfectly generated fibre. Flatness comes from writing R_S as the filtered colimit of the fractional ideals R_D over the monoid of effective divisors supported on S, each of which is projective; the same description gives the derived-localisation property; and the fibre is a filtered colimit of the perfect S-infinity-torsion modules R_D/R.
items.locator: Lemma 2.1.2, pp. 33-34; the notions are Definition [II].A.4.2

items.name: The localisation Poincare-Verdier sequence
items.statement: Let R be Dedekind and M a line bundle over R with R-linear involution, regarded as a Z-module with involution. For every m the sequence of Poincare infinity-categories (D^p_S(R), Q^{>=m}_M) -> (D^p(R), Q^{>=m}_M) -> (D^p(R_S), Q^{>=m}_{M_S}) is a Poincare-Verdier sequence, where M_S is the localised line bundle; in particular it induces fibre sequences of GW- and L-spectra. Extension of scalars is a Poincare functor, so D^p_S(R) is closed under the duality induced by M and is a Poincare subcategory with the restricted structure.
items.locator: Proposition 2.1.3, p. 34; that GW and L are Verdier-localising is Corollary [II].4.5.1 and Corollary [II].4.4.x
items.note: The first of the two ingredients of Theorem 7. Note the hypothesis that M be a LINE BUNDLE with R-linear involution, which is stronger than being an invertible Z-module with involution and is what makes the localised module again of the same type.

items.name: The t-structure on torsion modules and the induced duality
items.statement: (i) The canonical t-structure on D(R) restricts to one on D^p_S(R), whose heart is the abelian category Tor^f_S(R) of finitely generated S-infinity-torsion R-modules. (ii) For T in that heart, the space of Q^s_{M[1]}(T) is discrete and naturally isomorphic to the abelian group of symmetric M_S/M-valued bilinear forms on T. (iii) For such T one has D_{M[1]}(T) = Hom_R(T, M_S/M); in particular D_{M[1]} restricts to a duality on the heart.
items.note: This is what puts the torsion category in the situation of Corollary 1.3.8, and hence is where the general-C form of the symmetric surgery proposition is actually needed.

items.name: The boundary map on Witt classes via dual lattices
items.statement: Let V be a finitely generated projective R_S-module with a unimodular symmetric form b valued in M_S, let P be an integral R-lattice in V and T = P^*/P. Then the boundary map sends the class of (V,b) to the class of (T,c) in L_0(D^p_S(R), Q^s_M[1]). The proof follows the description of the boundary map from Paper II: restrict b to P to get a hermitian lift, note that the bilinear part identifies the dual lattice P^* with D_M(P) so that the form's associated map is the inclusion of P in P^*, view (P,b_P) as a surgery datum on 0 with respect to Q^s_M[1], and carry out the surgery, which produces a Poincare form c on the cofibre P^*/P.
items.locator: Proposition 2.1.5, pp. 35-36; the description of the boundary map is Proposition [II].4.4.8
items.note: The concrete, lattice-theoretic description of the boundary map that makes the localisation sequence computable; it is what Lemma 2.2.9 then evaluates on one-dimensional forms.

items.name: When a hermitian functor between symmetric structures is Poincare
items.statement: In the notation of section 2.2, the hermitian functor (f^*, psi) from (D^p(B), Q^s_N) to (D^p(A), Q^s_M) is Poincare if and only if the map N -> f^*(M) induced by Psi, by restricting to one of the A-module structures, is an equivalence in D(B). Since D^p(B) is generated by B under finite colimits and retracts it suffices to check the relevant natural transformation on B, where it becomes the image under f_* of the given map, and f_* is conservative.

items.name: The restriction of the module along a residue map
items.statement: Let p be a non-zero prime in a Dedekind ring R and p : R -> F_p the quotient map. Then there is a canonical equivalence p^*(M) ≃ (p^{-1}M/M)[-1], and any choice of uniformiser for the prime determines an isomorphism p^{-1}M/M ≅ M/pM = p_!(M). The first comes from applying hom_R(-,M) to the fibre sequence of the prime ideal, and the second from passing to the local ring at the prime, where a uniformiser generates the valuation ideal.
items.note: The source of the degree shift in Theorem 7: the residue-field GW-spectrum appears with its module shifted by [-1], and only a choice of uniformiser turns that into the more familiar M/pM.

items.name: Restriction of scalars along a residue map is a Poincare functor
items.statement: Let p be a non-zero prime in a Dedekind ring and p : R -> F_p the quotient. For any line bundle M over R the restriction of scalars p_* : D^p(F_p) -> D^p(R) canonically refines to a Poincare functor (D^p(F_p), Q^s_{p^*M}) -> (D^p_S(R), Q^s_M). One applies Lemma 2.2.1 to the unit of the adjunction, using that p^*M is an invertible F_p-module by Lemma 2.2.2, and then observes that the image of p_* lies in the S-torsion subcategory.

items.name: The devissage theorem
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring, S a set of non-zero primes, and M a line bundle over R with R-linear involution. Then for every m in Z the direct sum Poincare functor from the sum over the primes of S of (D^p(F_p), (Q^s_{p^*M})[m]) to (D^p_S(R), (Q^s_M)[m]) induces a canonical equivalence on algebraic K-theory, GW-theory and L-theory spectra.
items.note: The hermitian analogue of Quillen's devissage. The proof reduces by the fibre sequence of Paper II to K-theory and L-theory, then to finite S by filtered colimits, then puts both sides in the situation of Corollary 1.3.8 using the t-structures - the left side being a product of perfect derived categories of fields and the right the torsion category of Lemma 2.1.4 - and finishes by checking that the functor is an isomorphism on symmetric and anti-symmetric Witt groups, which is the classical devissage of Quebbemann-Scharlau-Schulte.

items.name: Theorem 7 in its general form: the localisation-devissage fibre sequences
items.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem 2.2.4, restriction and localisation yield canonical fibre sequences of spectra, for every m in Z: the sum over the primes of S of GW(F_p; (Q^s_{p^*M})[m]) -> GW(R; (Q^s_M)[m]) -> GW(R_S; (Q^s_{M_S})[m]), and likewise for L-theory.
items.locator: Corollary 2.2.5, p. 39; this is Theorem 7 of the introduction in its choice-free form
items.note: The formulation independent of choices of uniformisers that the introduction promises alongside the more familiar shifted form.

items.name: The familiar form after choosing uniformisers, and naturality
items.statement: Using Lemma 2.2.2, after choosing uniformisers for the primes of S one obtains the more familiar fibre sequence with the sum over S of GW(F_p; (Q^s_{p_!M})[m-1]) in the fibre, and likewise for L-theory. For naturality: given a map of Dedekind rings f : R -> R', a line bundle M on R and a set S of primes, setting M' = R' (x)_R M and S' the primes whose preimage lies in S, there is a canonical commutative square of localisation maps inducing a map on horizontal fibres. In the case S a single prime, each prime of S' gives a residue map of fields with a corresponding identification of modules, but the induced map on fibres is NOT in general the one induced by that residue map and identification, unless a uniformiser for the prime is sent to a uniformiser upstairs.
items.note: A genuine subtlety for a design job: the naturality of the localisation sequence in the ring is not the naive one, precisely because the identification of the fibre term depends on a choice of uniformiser.

items.name: Prior art for the localisation-devissage sequence
items.statement: A variant of Corollary 2.2.5 for L-theory of short complexes in non-negative degrees - which for Dedekind rings coincides with symmetric L-theory there, by Theorem 1.2.22 and Corollary 1.3.14 - was proved by Ranicki. For Grothendieck-Witt theory, Hornbostel and Schlichting prove a devissage statement and obtain a localisation sequence of this type under the assumption that 2 is a unit. Apart from Schlichting's announcement, which provides the fibre sequence for GW after passing to connective covers, the authors are not aware of any previous results for Grothendieck-Witt spaces of this kind for rings in which 2 is not invertible.
items.note: Fixes exactly what is new: the novelty is the absence of any hypothesis on 2, and the statement at the spectrum rather than the connective-cover level.

items.name: Devissage is special to the symmetric structure, and fails only dyadically
items.statement: The devissage result is a special feature of the symmetric Poincare structure: among the Q^{>=m}_M it is the only one for which it holds at the spectrum level rather than merely in a range of degrees. By Corollary 1.2.12 it suffices to see that devissage fails for quadratic L-theory, and explicitly the maps Omega L^q(F_2) -> L^q(Z) -> L^q(Z[1/2]) cannot be part of a fibre sequence, since that would force L^q_2(Z) = 0, which is false; here one uses L^q_2(Z[1/2]) ≅ L^s_2(Z[1/2]) = 0 and the vanishing of L^q_3(F_2) from Remark 1.3.5. However devissage in quadratic L-theory fails only at dyadic primes, that is those containing 2.
items.note: An important negative result with an explicit counterexample, and the reason the paper works with GW^s throughout rather than with the genuine flavours: only the symmetric structure has devissage on the nose.

items.name: The boundary map on one-dimensional forms over a local Dedekind ring
items.statement: Let R be a local Dedekind ring with maximal ideal p, residue field F_p and fraction field K, let pi be a uniformiser and u a unit. Then the boundary map sends the one-dimensional form of pi times u to the one-dimensional form of the class of u in the residue field. The proof shows first that the boundary class of the form of a generator a of p is represented by the torsion module p^{-1}/R with the symmetric K/R-valued pairing sending a pair of classes to the class of a times their product, and second that under the devissage equivalence this corresponds to the same vector space with the corresponding p^{-1}/R-valued form.

items.name: Identification of the boundary with the classical second residue map
items.statement: Lemma 2.2.9 identifies the boundary map from L^s_0(K) to the sum over the primes of L^s_0(F_p) with the map induced by the maps on symmetric Witt groups constructed in Milnor-Husemoller, Chapter IV, section 1.
items.note: The bridge to the classical literature: the paper’s abstract boundary map is the classical second residue homomorphism, which is what makes the computations of section 2.3 possible.

items.name: The symmetric L-groups of a Dedekind ring away from characteristic 2
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring whose fraction field K is not of characteristic 2, and let I be the finite set of dyadic primes of R. Then L^s_n(R) is: the symmetric Witt group W^s(R) for n congruent 0 mod 4; the sum over the dyadic primes of W^s(F_p) for n congruent 1 mod 4; zero for n congruent 2 mod 4; and the cokernel of the boundary map for n congruent 3 mod 4.
items.note: The proof combines Corollary 1.2.16 and Corollary 1.3.14 for the degree-0 case, then uses that the symmetric L-groups of K and of each residue field vanish in odd degrees (Corollary 1.3.4) to cut the long exact sequence of Corollary 2.2.5 into four-term exact sequences; the n congruent 2 case uses that the anti-symmetric Witt group of K vanishes when char K is not 2, and the rest uses that symmetric L-theory of a characteristic-2 field is 2-periodic while for odd characteristic it vanishes in odd degrees.

items.name: The symmetric L-groups over a global field, explicitly
items.statement: Under the assumptions of Proposition 2.3.1, if in addition K is a global field and d is the finite number of dyadic primes of R, then L^s_n(R) is W^s(R) for n congruent 0 mod 4, (Z/2)^d for n congruent 1 mod 4, zero for n congruent 2 mod 4, and Pic(R)/2 for n congruent 3 mod 4.
items.note: The (Z/2)^d comes from the residue fields being finite of characteristic 2, whose symmetric Witt group is Z/2. The Pic(R)/2 comes from identifying the boundary with the classical second residue map (Remark 2.2.10) and quoting Milnor-Husemoller for number fields, extended to general global fields by Scharlau.

items.name: The symmetric L-groups in characteristic 2
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring whose fraction field is a global field of characteristic 2. Then L^s_n(R) is W^s(R) for n even and Pic(R)/2 for n odd. Here the L-groups are 2-periodic because R is an F_2-algebra, all residue fields are finite of characteristic 2, and the identification of the odd groups runs through the exact sequence relating the units of K, the divisor group and the Picard group.

items.name: The localisation-completion Poincare-Verdier square
items.statement: Let R be a ring, M invertible over R, and S the multiplicative set generated by an integer l in R; assume R^_l is the derived l-completion of R, for instance that the order of the l-infinity-torsion in R is bounded, or that l is not a zero divisor. Then the square relating (D^p(R),Q^{>=m}_M), (D^p(R^_l), Q^{>=m}), (D^c(R[1/l]), Q^{>=m}) and (D^{c'}(R^_l[1/l]), Q^{>=m}) is a Poincare-Verdier square for every m, where c and c' are the images of the respective K_0-groups; in particular it becomes a pullback after applying GW or L.
items.locator: Proposition 2.3.6, p. 43; the criterion is Proposition [II].4.5.5
items.note: The arithmetic fracture square in hermitian form: it is what lets the quadratic computations be assembled from the 2-complete and the 2-inverted pieces, and it is the engine of Proposition 2.3.9.

items.name: Quadratic L-theory is insensitive to I-adic completion
items.statement: Let R be a ring complete in the I-adic topology for an ideal I. Then the canonical map L^q(R) -> L^q(R/I) is an equivalence. The proof shows that the functor on unimodular quadratic forms induces a bijection on isomorphism classes: surjectivity because Proj(R) -> Proj(R/I) is full and essentially surjective, the form functor is surjective on pi_0, and unimodularity is detected modulo I by Nakayama's lemma since I lies in the Jacobson radical; injectivity by quoting Wall's theorem that an isometry of the induced forms lifts.
items.locator: Proposition 2.3.7, pp. 43-44; the lifting of isometries is quoted from [Wal70, Theorem 2]
items.note: This is what reduces the 2-complete quadratic computations to computations over the residue field, for instance L^q_0(Z^_2) to L^q_0(F_2).

items.name: The quadratic L-groups of a Dedekind ring away from characteristic 2
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring whose fraction field K is not of characteristic 2, with I the finite set of dyadic primes. Then L^q_n(R) is the quadratic Witt group W^q(R) for n congruent 0 mod 4, zero for n congruent 1 mod 4, and the sum over the dyadic primes of W^q(F_p) for n congruent 2 mod 4, the isomorphism in the last case being induced by the canonical maps R -> F_p. For n congruent 3 mod 4 there is a short exact sequence 0 -> A -> L^q_n(R) -> L^s_n(R) -> 0, where A is the total cokernel of the commutative square relating L^q_0 and L^s_0 of R and of its 2-completion.
items.note: Proved by mapping the quadratic localisation-completion square of Proposition 2.3.6 to the symmetric one, giving a cube whose analysis yields the four cases.

items.name: The quadratic L-groups over a number field, explicitly
items.statement: Under the assumptions of Proposition 2.3.9, if in addition K is a number field and d is the number of dyadic primes, then L^q_n(R) is W^q(R) for n congruent 0 mod 4, zero for n congruent 1 mod 4, and (Z/2)^d for n congruent 2 mod 4, the invariants in the last case being the Arf invariants of the images in the L-theory of the residue fields at the dyadic primes. Moreover there is an exact sequence 0 -> A -> L^q_{-1}(R) -> Pic(R)/2 -> 0 with A as in Proposition 2.3.9 and A a finite 2-group.
items.note: The identification of A as a finite 2-group uses that (2) factors into the dyadic primes, so that L^s_0 of the 2-completion is a finite product over them, and that each local map to the 2-inverted ring is injective.

items.name: The quadratic L-groups of the integers
items.statement: For R = Z the pullback square gives an exact sequence 0 -> L^q_0(Z) -> L^q_0(Z^_2) (+) L^s_0(Z) -> L^s_0(Z^_2) -> L^q_{-1}(Z) -> 0 in which the map L^q_0(Z) -> L^q_0(Z^_2) is zero and the map L^q_0(Z) -> L^s_0(Z) is multiplication by 8. The first holds because, by Proposition 2.3.7, it suffices to know the map L^q_0(Z) -> L^q_0(F_2) is zero, and the Arf invariant of the E_8-form viewed over F_2 is zero; the second because the E_8-form generates L^q_0(Z). One therefore gets a short exact sequence 0 -> Z/2 (+) Z/8 -> L^s_0(Z^_2) -> L^q_{-1}(Z) -> 0. By localisation-devissage there is a short exact sequence 0 -> L^s_0(Z^_2) -> L^s_0(Q_2) -> Z/2 -> 0, and since L^s_0(Q_2) has 32 elements, L^s_0(Z^_2) has 16.
items.locator: Example 2.3.13, p. 46; the order of L^s_0(Q_2) is quoted from Lam
items.note: The concrete arithmetic input to Theorem 4: the vanishing of the Arf invariant of E_8 over F_2 and the order 32 of the symmetric Witt group of the 2-adic numbers. Note this example also supplies the groups used in Remark 1.2.13 to show the comparison range of Corollary 1.2.12 is optimal.

items.name: A worked example over the Eisenstein integers
items.statement: For K the quadratic field obtained by adjoining the square root of -3 to the rationals and R its ring of integers - the Eisenstein integers, a euclidean hence principal ideal domain - the discriminant is (3), and since (2) does not divide (3) the ideal (2) is prime and is the single dyadic prime. Hence L^s_2(R) = L^s_3(R) = 0, the Picard group of a principal ideal domain vanishing, while L^s_1(R) ≅ Z/2 and L^s_0(R) ≅ W^s(R) ≅ Z/4. The quadratic L-groups are then computed from a diagram of exact sequences comparing the situation over Z with that over R, identifying A with the cokernel of the comparison map.
items.locator: Example 2.3.14, pp. 46-47; the Witt group Z/4 is quoted from Milnor-Husemoller and the primality of (2) from Neukirch

items.name: Finite generation of the symmetric and quadratic L-groups of number rings
items.statement: Let O be a number ring, that is a localisation of the ring of integers in a number field away from finitely many primes, and epsilon = +/-1. Then the epsilon-symmetric L-groups L^s_n(O;epsilon) and the epsilon-quadratic L-groups L^q_n(O;epsilon) are finitely generated. By the computations above it suffices to show that the symmetric Witt group, the quadratic Witt group and the Picard group of O are finitely generated; the symmetric Witt group is an extension of a finite group by a free abelian group whose rank is the number of real embeddings of the field.
items.locator: Corollary 2.3.16, pp. 47-48; the Witt-group finiteness is quoted from [MH73, section 4, Theorem 4.1]

items.name: Finite generation for every flavour, and for Grothendieck-Witt groups
items.statement: Let O be a number ring and epsilon = +/-1. Then for all m,n the groups L_n(O;Q^{>=m}_epsilon), and consequently the groups GW_n(O;Q^{>=m}_epsilon), are finitely generated. Since Q^{>=m}_epsilon is m-quadratic and (2-m)-symmetric, Corollary 1.2.12 gives that L^q_n(O;epsilon) -> L_n(O;Q^{>=m}_epsilon) is surjective for n <= 2m-2, and Corollary 1.3.9 gives that L_n(O;Q^{>=m}_epsilon) -> L^s_n(O;epsilon) is injective for n >= 2m-1; in both ranges the comparison group is finitely generated by Corollary 2.3.16. The Grothendieck-Witt consequence then follows from the fibre sequence together with Quillen's theorem that the algebraic K-groups of number rings are finitely generated.
items.locator: Corollary 2.3.18, p. 48; the K-theory finiteness is quoted from Quillen
items.note: A neat use of the two comparison ranges in opposite directions: quadratic surjects onto the flavour below the range, and the flavour injects into symmetric above it, so finite generation propagates to every m and n.

items.name: Corollary 8: finite generation of the classical Grothendieck-Witt groups
items.statement: Let O be a number ring and epsilon = +/-1. Then the classical epsilon-symmetric and epsilon-quadratic Grothendieck-Witt groups GW^s_{cl,n}(O;epsilon) and GW^q_{cl,n}(O;epsilon) are finitely generated for all n >= 0.
items.locator: Corollary 2.3.19, p. 48; announced as Corollary 8 in the introduction

items.name: The homological stability route, and why it does not reach the symmetric case
items.statement: The finite generation of the quadratic Grothendieck-Witt groups can also be deduced by a homological stability argument analogous to Quillen's for algebraic K-theory of number rings: by Serre class theory it suffices to show the ordinary homology groups of the components of the infinite loop space are finitely generated, and since every epsilon-quadratic form is a direct summand of an epsilon-hyperbolic form, the group completion theorem identifies any such component with the plus construction on the colimit of the automorphism groups - the infinite orthogonal group for epsilon = 1 and the infinite quadratic symplectic group for epsilon = -1. In the generality presented here the argument is not known to carry over to the symmetric case.
items.note: This is the explicit statement the introduction refers to for why Corollary 8 needs the paper’s methods in the symmetric case: the classical route works only for the quadratic one.

items.name: The (-1)-symmetric L-groups follow by double suspension
items.statement: There is a canonical equivalence between the (-1)-symmetric L-theory spectrum of R and the double suspension of its symmetric L-theory spectrum, so Proposition 2.3.1 and Corollary 2.3.2 also determine the (-1)-symmetric L-groups.

items.name: The symmetric L-groups of a local Dedekind ring
items.statement: Let R be a local Dedekind ring with fraction field K and residue field k. Then the boundary map from L^s_0(K) to L^s_0(k) is surjective by Lemma 2.2.9 and its kernel is L^s_0(R). If the characteristic of K is not 2, then L^s_n(R) vanishes for n congruent 2 or 3 mod 4, and for n congruent 1 mod 4 it is the symmetric Witt group of k when k has characteristic 2 and trivial otherwise. If the characteristic of K is 2, then L^s_1(R) = 0.

items.name: Quadratic L-theory is insensitive to henselian pairs
items.statement: Let F be a functor from commutative rings to spectra commuting with filtered colimits such that for every Noetherian commutative ring R complete in the I-adic topology the map F(R) -> F(R/I) is an equivalence. Then F(S) -> F(S/J) is an equivalence for every henselian pair (S,J). Since L-theory commutes with filtered colimits, it follows from Proposition 2.3.7 that L^q(S) -> L^q(S/J) is an equivalence for every henselian pair.
items.locator: Remark 2.3.8, p. 44; the authors thank Akhil Mathew and refer to [CMM21, Remark 5.6]

items.name: The (-1)-quadratic L-groups follow by double suspension
items.statement: As in the symmetric case there is a canonical equivalence between the (-1)-quadratic L-theory spectrum of R and the double suspension of its quadratic L-theory spectrum, so Proposition 2.3.9 and Corollary 2.3.10 also determine the (-1)-quadratic L-groups.

items.name: The correction term A is non-trivial as soon as there are two dyadic primes
items.statement: If the number d of dyadic primes of R is at least 2 then the group A of Proposition 2.3.9 is not trivial: taking the rank modulo 2 gives surjections from L^s_0(R) to Z/2 and from L^s_0 of the 2-completion to (Z/2)^d under which both horizontal composites out of the quadratic L-groups vanish, so that one obtains surjections of the two cokernels, and the induced map on vertical cokernels is a surjection from A onto (Z/2)^{d-1}.

items.name: Devissage does hold in quadratic L-theory away from the dyadic primes
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring and S a set of primes containing no dyadic prime, so that R and its localisation have the same 2-adic completion. Then in the square comparing the quadratic and symmetric L-theories of R, of the localisation and of the 2-completion, the outer and the right squares are pullbacks by the proof of Proposition 2.3.9, hence so is the left one; and since the residue field at a non-dyadic prime has odd characteristic, so that its quadratic and symmetric L-theories agree, Corollary 2.2.5 gives a fibre sequence from L^q(R) to the quadratic L-theory of the localisation with cofibre the sum of the L^q of the residue fields. The failure of devissage in quadratic L-theory is therefore a purely dyadic phenomenon.

items.name: The characteristic 2 case of the Witt-group input
items.statement: For a Dedekind ring R whose fraction field K has characteristic 2 one finds instead that the map from the symmetric Witt group of R to that of K is injective, by the same argument as in odd characteristic since over a field of characteristic 2 a form is zero in the symmetric Witt group if and only if it admits a strict Lagrangian; but the map from the quadratic to the symmetric Witt group of R is zero, because the composite to the symmetric Witt group of K factors through the corresponding map for K, which vanishes since the underlying bilinear form of a quadratic form over a field of characteristic 2 has a symplectic basis and hence a Lagrangian.

items.name: The homotopy limit problem for fields of finite virtual mod 2 cohomological dimension
items.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic different from 2 such that the virtual mod 2 cohomological dimension vcd_2(k) is finite, where vcd_2(k) is by definition the ordinary mod 2 cohomological dimension of the absolute Galois group of k adjoined a square root of -1, so that vcd_2(k) <= cd_2(k). Then for epsilon = +/-1 the map of spectra GW^s(k;epsilon) -> K(k;epsilon)^{hC_2} is an equivalence after 2-completion, where K(k;epsilon) carries the C_2-action induced by the duality hom_k(-,k(epsilon)).
items.locator: Theorem 3.1.1, p. 49; quoted from [HKO11] in characteristic 0, [BKSO15] in positive odd characteristic, with an alternative proof in [BH20]
items.note: Recalled as the state of the art for fields; the paper uses it as input and extends it to Dedekind rings in Theorem 3.1.7.

items.name: Comparison with Schlichting’s model, and the history of the field case
items.statement: Theorem 3.1.1 was stated in [BKSO15] in terms of Schlichting's model for Grothendieck-Witt spectra; since the characteristic is not 2 the comparison statement of Proposition [II].B.2.2 identifies that construction with the one used here. The special case of the complex numbers reduces to the classical equivalence BO ~ BU^{hC_2}, proved in [BK05, Lemma 7.3] also in the (-1)-symmetric variant, and the case of the complex numbers in turn implies the case of finite fields.
items.locator: Remark 3.1.2 with the discussion following it, pp. 49-50

items.name: The homotopy limit problem for finite fields
items.statement: For epsilon = +/-1 and every prime power q the natural map GW^s_{cl}(F_q;epsilon) -> K(F_q;epsilon)^{hC_2} is an equivalence on connective covers. This follows by expressing the Grothendieck-Witt spaces of F_q in terms of Adams operations on BO and BSp, in analogy with Quillen's computation of the algebraic K-theory of F_q, combined with the positive solution of the homotopy limit problem for the complex numbers.
items.locator: Theorem 3.1.3, p. 50; the input is [Fri76] as corrected and expanded in [FP78]
items.note: The paper points out that [FP78] corrected a mistake of [Fri76]: Friedlander computed pi_1(GW^q_{cl}(F_q)) to be trivial for q even, whereas it is in fact Z/2. That is an erratum in the cited literature, not in this paper.

items.name: A short proof of the homotopy limit problem for finite fields of even order
items.statement: Let q = 2^r for a positive integer r. Then the map of spectra GW(F_q;(Q^s)[m]) -> K(F_q;(Q^s)[m])^{hC_2} is an equivalence for every integer m. By the cartesian square of Corollary [II].4.4.13 it suffices to show that L(F_q;(Q^s)[m]) -> K(F_q;(Q^s)[m])^{tC_2} is an equivalence; the metabolic sequence reduces this to m = 0, 2-periodicity reduces it to degrees 0 and 1, and Quillen's computation that the K-groups of a finite field are odd torsion in positive degrees identifies the Tate term with the Tate construction on the integers. One then checks that the generating symmetric bilinear form maps to a generator.
items.note: This proposition, not merely Theorem 3.1.3, is what the proof of Theorem 3.1.7 uses, because it covers the spectrum and all shifts, not only the connective space.

items.name: A multiplicative proof of the same statement
items.statement: An alternative argument for Proposition 3.1.4 uses multiplicative structures: Paper [IV] shows that L(R;Q^s) -> K(R;Q^s)^{tC_2} is a map of E_infinity-rings for a commutative ring R, and for R = F_q with q even both homotopy rings are the Laurent polynomial ring over F_2 on a generator in degree 2, every ring endomorphism of which is an isomorphism.

items.name: The homotopy limit problem for perfect fields of characteristic 2
items.statement: Let k be a perfect field of characteristic 2. Then the map F_2 -> k induces an equivalence on 2-complete K-theory, by an analysis of Adams operations, and on L-theory, since the odd L-groups vanish for both and the map is an isomorphism on symmetric Witt groups: every element of the Witt group of a field is a sum of one-dimensional forms, and perfectness makes every such form isomorphic to the unit form, so that the rank modulo 2 map from the symmetric Witt group to Z/2 is an isomorphism. Hence the homotopy limit problem has an affirmative answer for every perfect field of characteristic 2.
items.locator: Remark 3.1.6, pp. 51-52; the K-theory input is [Hil81, Theorem 5.4]

items.name: Theorem 2: the homotopy limit problem for Dedekind rings with number-field fraction field
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring whose fraction field is a number field. Then for every integer m and every line bundle M over R with involution +/-1, the map GW(R;(Q^s_M)[m]) -> K(R;(Q^s_M)[m])^{hC_2} is a 2-adic equivalence. Combined with Corollary 1.3.15, which makes GW^s_{cl}(R;M) -> GW(R;Q^s_M) an equivalence in non-negative degrees, this gives Theorem 2 of the introduction. The proof maps the localisation-devissage sequence at the set S of primes over 2 to its K-theoretic counterpart: the left-hand map is an equivalence by Proposition 3.1.4 since the residue fields at dyadic primes are finite of characteristic 2, and the right-hand map is a 2-adic equivalence by [BKSO15, Theorem 2.2], the residue fields of R[1/2] being finite fields or a number field and hence of finite virtual mod 2 cohomological dimension.
items.note: This is where the hermitian localisation-devissage sequence of Theorem 7 pays for itself: it lets the dyadic primes, where 2 is not invertible and the earlier literature does not apply, be treated by the finite-field case.

items.name: The conclusion for all global fields of characteristic different from 2
items.statement: The conclusion of Theorem 3.1.7 therefore holds for every Dedekind ring whose field of fractions is a global field of characteristic different from 2: in the odd characteristic case [BKSO15] applies directly, and the characteristic zero case is Theorem 3.1.7.

items.name: When the 2-adic equivalence is an integral equivalence
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring with global fraction field K of characteristic different from 2. If K is not formally real, that is if -1 is a sum of squares - equivalently K has positive odd characteristic or is a totally imaginary number field - then the symmetric Witt group of K is 2-primary torsion of bounded exponent, hence L^s(R) is derived 2-complete, and since the Tate term is 2-complete the map of Theorem 3.1.7 is an equivalence before 2-completion. Conversely, if K admits a real embedding then for every line bundle M the group W^s(R;M) contains the integers as a direct summand, so L^s(R;M) is not 2-complete and the map is not an integral equivalence; equivalently L^s(R) contains L^s of the reals as a retract.
items.locator: Remark 3.1.9, p. 52; the Witt-group input is [Sch85, Theorem 2.7.9] and the retract is [HLN20, Theorem A]

items.name: A 2-adic local variant beyond the stated hypotheses
items.statement: The proof of Theorem 3.1.7 shows the hypotheses are not optimal. Let R be the ring of integers in a non-archimedean local field K of mixed characteristic (0,2) with residue field k, for instance a dyadic completion of a number ring; then M is trivial since R is local. Since cd_2(K) = 2 the right-hand vertical map in the localisation square is a 2-adic equivalence, so the middle map is a 2-adic equivalence if and only if the residue-field map is. If k is finite the middle map is a 2-adic equivalence, and since then K is a finite extension of the 2-adic numbers, whose symmetric L-theory is 2-power torsion, it is in fact an equivalence.
items.locator: Remark 3.1.10, pp. 52-53; the cohomological dimension is [Ser02, section 4.3] and the torsion statement [Lam05, Theorem VI 2.29]

items.name: The Berrick-Karoubi conjecture: inverting 2 is harmless 2-locally
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring whose fraction field is a global field of characteristic zero. Then the map GW^s(R;epsilon) -> GW^s(R[1/2];epsilon) is a 2-local equivalence on connected covers and injective on pi_0. In the case of the integers this was conjectured by Berrick and Karoubi. The proof identifies the fibre with a sum of terms GW(F_p;(Q^s_epsilon)[-1]) over the dyadic primes, shows each is an equivalence onto the homotopy fixed points by Proposition 3.1.4, and deduces from Quillen's computation that the comparison map to the integers with sign action is 1-connective and a 2-local equivalence.
items.locator: Proposition 3.1.11 with its proof, p. 53; the conjecture is from [BK05]

items.name: A mod 2 variant for perfect dyadic residue fields
items.statement: Let R be a Dedekind ring of characteristic zero all of whose residue fields at dyadic primes are perfect. Then the map GW^s(R;epsilon)/2 -> GW^s(R[1/2];epsilon)/2 is (-1)-truncated; for this one needs only that K(k)/2 is 0-truncated for a perfect field k of characteristic 2, that is that the higher K-groups are uniquely 2-divisible. This does not in general imply that they vanish after localisation at 2, but it does for instance for an algebraic closure of F_2, and whenever the 2-local K-theory of the residue field is the 2-local integers the argument of Proposition 3.1.11 applies verbatim. Every perfect field of positive characteristic p is the residue field of a characteristic 0 Dedekind ring, namely the ring of p-typical Witt vectors.

items.name: An obstruction to the homotopy limit problem for classical Grothendieck-Witt theory
items.statement: Suppose that the map GW^s_{cl}(R;M)/2 -> K(R)^{hC_2}/2 is n-truncated for some natural number n, where the source is viewed as a connective spectrum. Then the map L^{gs}(R;M) -> L^s(R;M) is (n-1)-truncated. In particular GW^s_{cl}(R)/2 -> K(R)^{hC_2}/2 cannot be an equivalence in non-negative degrees unless the comparison map of genuine to non-genuine symmetric L-theory is, and Example 1.3.11 exhibits rings for which it is not.
items.locator: Proposition 3.1.13 with its proof, pp. 53-54; the 0-truncatedness input is [HS21]
items.note: The proof runs the pullback square modulo 2 and then uses that L^{gs} is a filtered colimit along shift maps whose colimit is L^s, comparing with the 4-periodicity of the Tate term.

items.name: 2-inverted L-theory does not see the flavour
items.statement: Let R be a ring with invertible Z-module with involution M, and let m be an integer or plus or minus infinity. Then the natural map L(R;Q^{>=m}_M)[1/2] -> L(R;Q^s_M)[1/2] is an equivalence. The proof uses that L^{gs}(Z) -> L^s(Z) is an equivalence after inverting 2, that the shift maps are multiplication by the class in L^{gs}_4(Z) of the integers shifted by -2 with their standard genuine symmetric structure of signature 1, and hence that L(R;Q^s_M) is the base change of L(R;Q^{>=m}_M) along L^{gs}(Z) -> L^s(Z).
items.locator: Proposition 3.1.14 with its proof, p. 54; multiplicative structures on L-theory are developed in Paper [IV]
items.note: Together with Karoubi’s splitting this is why all flavour comparisons in the paper are purely 2-primary phenomena.

items.name: The classical symmetric Grothendieck-Witt group of the integers in degree 0, and its plus construction
items.statement: GW^s_{cl}(Z) is the homotopy theoretic group completion of the maximal subgroupoid of non-degenerate symmetric bilinear forms over the integers. By Serre there is an isomorphism pi_0 GW^s_{cl}(Z) = Z (+) Z, the summands generated by the rank one forms <1> and <-1>. Writing O_{<n,n>}(Z) for the automorphism group of the n-fold orthogonal sum of <1> perp <-1> inside GL_{2n}(Z) and O_{<infinity,infinity>}(Z) for the colimit, that group has perfect commutator subgroup and every non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form over the integers is an orthogonal summand of such a sum, so the group completion theorem gives an equivalence of spaces between the positive part of GW^s_{cl}(Z) and the plus construction on the classifying space of O_{<infinity,infinity>}(Z).
items.locator: Section 3.2, p. 54, case (1)-symmetric; quoted from [Ser61, Theoremes 1 and 4], [RW13, Proposition 3.1 and Corollary 1.2] and [MS76]

items.name: The classical symplectic Grothendieck-Witt group of the integers in degree 0
items.statement: GW^{-s}_{cl}(Z) is the group completion of the maximal subgroupoid of non-degenerate symplectic bilinear forms over the integers. Since every symplectic form over the integers is an orthogonal sum of copies of the standard symplectic form on the square of the integers, pi_0 GW^{-s}_{cl}(Z) = Z generated by that form; the infinite symplectic group is perfect and the group completion theorem identifies the positive part of GW^{-s}_{cl}(Z) with the plus construction on its classifying space.

items.name: The classical quadratic Grothendieck-Witt group of the integers in degree 0
items.statement: GW^q_{cl}(Z) is the group completion of the maximal subgroupoid of non-degenerate quadratic forms over the integers. Writing H_q for the standard hyperbolic quadratic form and E_8 for the classical 8-dimensional form attached to the Dynkin diagram of that name, Serre's theorem that every quadratic form becomes, after adding one hyperbolic summand, a sum of copies of H_q and of E_8 gives pi_0 GW^q_{cl}(Z) = Z (+) Z with generators H_q and E_8. The infinite orthogonal group O_{infinity,infinity}(Z) of the hyperbolic quadratic forms has perfect commutator subgroup and the group completion theorem identifies the positive part of GW^q_{cl}(Z) with the plus construction on its classifying space.
items.locator: Section 3.2, p. 55, case (1)-quadratic; quoted from [Ser61, Theoreme 5]
items.note: The E_8-form is the element whose image under symmetrisation is 8 times a generator, which is the arithmetic content of Lemma 3.2.7 and of Example 2.3.13.

items.name: The classical (-1)-quadratic Grothendieck-Witt group of the integers in degree 0
items.statement: GW^{-q}_{cl}(Z) is built from (-1)-quadratic forms over the integers; such a form is determined by its rank, which is even, and its Arf invariant. Writing H^0_{-q} and H^1_{-q} for the standard hyperbolic (-1)-quadratic forms on the square of the integers with the standard alternating matrix and quadratic refinements xy and x^2+xy+y^2 respectively, every form of Arf invariant 0 is a sum of copies of H^0_{-q} and every form of Arf invariant 1 is a sum of copies of H^0_{-q} together with one copy of H^1_{-q}. Hence pi_0 GW^{-q}_{cl}(Z) = Z (+) Z/2, and with Sp^q_{2n}(Z) the subgroup of the symplectic group preserving the quadratic refinement, the group completion theorem identifies the positive part with the plus construction on the classifying space of Sp^q_{infinity}(Z).
items.locator: Section 3.2, p. 55, case (-1)-quadratic; the classification of forms is [Bro12, section III.1]

items.name: Bernoulli numbers, the numbers c_n and w_{2n}, and the K-groups of the integers
items.statement: The Bernoulli numbers are defined by the expansion of x/(e^x - 1). One writes c_n for the numerator of the absolute value of B_{2n}/4n, which is odd, and w_{2n} for its denominator. For every k >= 0 the order of K_{8k+2}(Z) is 2c_{2k+1} and the order of K_{8k+6}(Z) is c_{2k+2}, and there are isomorphisms K_{8k+3}(Z) = Z/2w_{4k+2} and K_{8k+7}(Z) = Z/w_{4k+4}.
items.locator: Section 3.2, p. 55; quoted from [Wei13, Theorem 10.1], resting on the resolution of the Quillen-Lichtenbaum conjecture by Rost and Voevodsky
items.note: Checked against the standard list: K_2 = Z/2 of order 2c_1, K_22 = Z/691 of order c_6 = 691, K_3 = Z/48 = Z/2w_2, K_7 = Z/240 = Z/w_4, K_11 = Z/1008 = Z/2w_6, K_23 = Z/65520 = Z/w_12.

items.name: The odd torsion in the K-groups of the integers is cyclic in the known range
items.statement: For an abelian group A write A_odd for its odd torsion subgroup. For m <= 5000 the group K_{4m-2}(Z)_odd is known to be cyclic of order c_m, and this holds for all m if the Kummer-Vandiver conjecture is true.
items.locator: Remark 3.2.1, p. 55; quoted from [Wei13, Example 10.3.2 and Theorem 10.2]
items.note: This is the one point at which the tables of Theorem 3.2.2 depend on an open conjecture; the groups themselves are determined, only their cyclicity is conditional.

items.name: Theorem 4: the symmetric and symplectic Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers
items.statement: The classical epsilon-symmetric Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers are given in degrees n >= 1 by the following table, in which k >= 0. For n = 8k: GW^s_{cl,n}(Z) = Z (+) Z/2 and GW^{-s}_{cl,n}(Z) = 0. For n = 8k+1: (Z/2)^3 and 0. For n = 8k+2: (Z/2)^2 (+) K_{8k+2}(Z)_odd and Z (+) K_{8k+2}(Z)_odd. For n = 8k+3: Z/w_{4k+2} and Z/2w_{4k+2}. For n = 8k+4: Z and Z/2. For n = 8k+5: 0 and Z/2. For n = 8k+6: K_{8k+6}(Z)_odd and Z (+) K_{8k+6}(Z)_odd. For n = 8k+7: Z/w_{4k+4} and Z/w_{4k+4}.
items.locator: Theorem 3.2.2 with the table on p. 56
items.note: Proof: since the groups are finitely generated it suffices to work 2-locally and after inverting 2. 2-locally, Proposition 3.1.11 and Corollary 1.3.15 make GW^s_{cl}(Z;epsilon) -> GW^s_{cl}(Z[1/2];epsilon) a 2-local equivalence in degrees >= 1, where [BK05, Theorem B] applies; comparing the 8k+3 and 8k+7 entries uses von Staudt’s theorem that the largest power of 2 dividing w_{2n} equals the largest power of 2 dividing 8n. After inverting 2 the fibre sequence of Theorem 1 splits, giving GW^s_n(Z;epsilon)[1/2] = L^s_n(Z;epsilon)[1/2] for n congruent 0,1 mod 4 and K_n(Z;epsilon)[1/2] (+) L^s_n(Z;epsilon)[1/2] for n congruent 2,3 mod 4. Transcribed from a rendered image of the page and checked entry by entry against both halves of that argument.

items.name: The odd-degree groups consist of image-of-J classes
items.statement: The number w_{2n} equals the cardinality of the image of the J-homomorphism from pi_{4n-1}(O) to pi_{4n-1} of the sphere spectrum, and by Quillen the unit map from the sphere to K(Z) is injective on that image. Since the unit map for K(Z) factors through the unit map for GW^s_{cl}(Z), the groups GW^s_{cl,8k+3}(Z) = Z/w_{4k+2} and GW^s_{cl,8k+7}(Z) = Z/w_{4k+4} consist precisely of image-of-J classes.
items.locator: Remark 3.2.3, p. 56; the injectivity is [Qui76, p. 186]

items.name: Galatius’s lemma: the duality acts by a sign on 2-inverted K-groups
items.statement: Let F be a number field and O a ring of S-integers in F. Then the C_2-actions induced by the Poincare structures Q^s and Q^s_- on the perfect derived category of O induce multiplication by (-1)^n on the groups K_{2n-1}(O)[1/2] and K_{2n-2}(O)[1/2] for each n >= 2. The proof reduces to l-completed K-groups for odd primes l, identifies them with etale K-theory of O[1/l], and reads the action off the etale descent spectral sequence, whose E_2-page is etale cohomology with l-adic Tate twists on which the dualisation action acts by (-1)^n; the spectral sequence collapses because the l-adic etale cohomological dimension is 2 and the degree zero cohomology of a positive twist vanishes.
items.locator: Lemma 3.2.4 with its proof, pp. 56-57; the authors thank Soren Galatius and point to [FGV22, section 2]; the etale comparison is [CM21, Theorems 1.2 and 1.3] and the identification of the homotopy sheaves uses results of Gabber and Suslin
items.note: This is the ingredient that makes the odd-primary part of every Grothendieck-Witt computation in the section purely a matter of taking C_2-invariants of K-groups.

items.name: Overlap with Schlichting’s announced calculation
items.statement: A calculation of the Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers has also been announced by Schlichting; see [Sch19] and the erratum [Sch24].

items.name: The first 24 Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers
items.statement: The first 24 non-negative Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers are as follows. For GW^s_k(Z), k = 0,...,23 in order: Z (+) Z; (Z/2)^3; (Z/2)^2; Z/24; Z; 0; 0; Z/240; Z (+) Z/2; (Z/2)^3; (Z/2)^2; Z/504; Z; 0; 0; Z/480; Z (+) Z/2; (Z/2)^3; (Z/2)^2; Z/264; Z; 0; Z/691; Z/65520. For GW^{-s}_k(Z), k = 0,...,23 in order: Z; 0; Z; Z/48; Z/2; Z/2; Z; Z/240; 0; 0; Z; Z/1008; Z/2; Z/2; Z; Z/480; 0; 0; Z; Z/528; Z/2; Z/2; Z (+) Z/691; Z/65520. The only information beyond the table of Theorem 3.2.2 is the structure of the odd torsion in K_n(Z) for n congruent 2 or 6 mod 8, the only non-trivial one in this range being K_22(Z) = Z/691.
items.locator: Proposition 3.2.6 and Table 1, p. 57; the list of K-groups is [Wei13, Example 10.3]

items.name: The cofibre of the symmetrisation map on genuine L-theory of the integers
items.statement: Write C for the cofibre of the map L^{gq}(Z) -> L^{gs}(Z) and C_i for its homotopy groups. Then C_1 = Z/2, C_0 = Z/8, C_{-1} = Z/2, and C_i = 0 for all other i. The proof compares L^q(Z), L^{gq}(Z), L^{gs}(Z) and L^s(Z): the maps from L^q are isomorphisms on homotopy in degrees at most 1 and at most -3 respectively, and the maps to L^s are isomorphisms in degrees at least 2 and at least -2 respectively, by Corollaries 1.2.12 and 1.3.9 together with the fact that Q^{gq} is 1-symmetric and Q^{gs} is 3-symmetric. With L^{gs}_{-2}(Z) = 0 this confines C to degrees -1 to 1; then C_{-1} = L^{gq}_{-2}(Z) = L^q_{-2}(Z) = Z/2, and the remaining two groups sit in the exact sequence 0 -> L^{gs}_1(Z) -> C_1 -> L^{gq}_0(Z) -> L^{gs}_0(Z) -> C_0 -> 0 in which the third map is multiplication by 8 on the integers, so C_0 = Z/8 and C_1 = L^{gs}_1(Z) = Z/2.
items.locator: Lemma 3.2.7 with its proof, p. 58; the value of L^{gs}_1(Z) is [Ran81, Proposition 4.3.1]

items.name: C is a truncation of normal, or hyperquadratic, L-theory
items.statement: Writing L^n(R) for the cofibre of the symmetrisation map L^q(R) -> L^s(R), called normal or hyperquadratic L-theory in Ranicki's work, one has C equivalent to the truncation of L^n(Z) in the interval from -1 to 1.

items.name: The classical quadratic Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers
items.statement: The classical quadratic Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers are GW^{gq}_0(Z) = Z (+) Z, freely generated by the standard hyperbolic form and the positive definite even form E_8; GW^{gq}_1(Z) = Z/2 (+) Z/2; and GW^{gq}_n(Z) = GW^{gs}_n(Z) for n >= 2. The proof of the middle case uses the exact sequence C_2 -> GW^{gq}_1(Z) -> GW^{gs}_1(Z) -> C_1 -> GW^{gq}_0(Z) -> GW^{gs}_0(Z), in which the last map is injective with image of index 8, so that GW^{gs}_1(Z) = (Z/2)^3 surjects onto C_1 = Z/2 and, since C_2 = 0, the group GW^{gq}_1(Z) is (Z/2)^2.

items.name: The symplectic cofibre is a double suspension of C
items.statement: Let D be the cofibre of the map L^{-gq}(Z) -> L^{-gs}(Z). Then D is equivalent to the double suspension of C, because the shift periodicity of Proposition R.6 and Remark R.4 give equivalences identifying L^{-gq}(Z) and L^{-gs}(Z) with the double suspensions of L^{gq}(Z) and L^{gs}(Z) compatibly with symmetrisation.

items.name: Two homotopy orbit groups of the symplectic K-theory of the integers
items.statement: There are isomorphisms pi_1 of K(Z;Q^{gq}_-)_{hC_2} = Z/4 and pi_2 of K(Z;Q^{gq}_-)_{hC_2} = 0. Since the involution depends only on the underlying duality one may replace the genuine quadratic structure by the symmetric one. For the first group the homotopy orbit spectral sequence gives order 4, because the second group homology of C_2 with coefficients in pi_0 vanishes so that the generator of the zeroth homology with coefficients in pi_1 is not an eventual boundary, and the first homology with coefficients in pi_0 contributes order 2; the exact sequence L^{-s}_2(Z) -> pi_1 K(Z;Q^s_-)_{hC_2} -> GW^{-s}_1(Z) with the outer groups the integers and zero then forces the middle group to be cyclic, hence Z/4. For the second group one compares with topological K- and Grothendieck-Witt theory of the reals: the map K(Z) -> K^{top}(R) = ko is an isomorphism on homotopy in degrees at most 2, so it suffices to see that pi_2 of K^{top}(R;Q^s_-)_{hC_2} vanishes, and that group sits between L^{top}_3(R;Q^s_-) = 0 and GW^{top}_2(R;Q^s_-) = pi_1 Sp^{top}_infinity(R) = Z, hence is free, while the spectral sequence bounds its order by 4.

items.name: Topological K-theory, Grothendieck-Witt theory and L-theory of the real numbers
items.statement: Following Schlichting one defines the topological variants of K-theory, Grothendieck-Witt theory and L-theory of the real numbers with their usual topology by applying the corresponding functor to the simplicial ring whose n-simplices are the continuous maps from the topological n-simplex to the reals with pointwise operations, and taking the geometric realisation, equivalently the colimit over the simplex category. The resulting map K^{top}(R) -> ko is an equivalence; GW^{top}_0(R;Q^s_epsilon) = GW_0(R;Q^s_epsilon) and the 1-connective cover of GW^{top}(R;Q^s_epsilon) is naturally equivalent to the topologised infinite orthogonal space for epsilon = 1 and to the topologised infinite symplectic space for epsilon = -1; and the natural map L(R;Q^s_epsilon) -> L^{top}(R;Q^s_epsilon) is an equivalence.
items.locator: Section 3.2, p. 59, within the proof of Lemma 3.2.11; quoted from [Sch17, section 10, Proposition 10.2 and Remark 10.4]

items.name: Karoubi periodicity reading of the previous lemma
items.statement: By Karoubi periodicity, K(Z;Q^s_-) is equivalent as a spectrum with C_2-action to the representation sphere S^{2-2sigma} tensored with K(Z;Q^s), and the map K(Z) -> ko is C_2-equivariant for the action induced by Q^s on the source and the trivial action on ko. Lemma 3.2.11 is therefore a statement about the low dimensional homotopy groups of the homotopy orbits of S^{2-2sigma} tensored with ko, which can also be computed from the cofibre sequence relating the free C_2-orbit, the sphere and the representation sphere S^sigma.
items.locator: Remark 3.2.12, p. 60; the periodicity is Corollary [II].4.6.4

items.name: The classical (-1)-quadratic Grothendieck-Witt groups of the integers
items.statement: There are isomorphisms GW^{-gq}_0(Z) = Z (+) Z/2, GW^{-gq}_1(Z) = Z/4, GW^{-gq}_2(Z) = Z, GW^{-gq}_3(Z) = Z/24, and GW^{-gq}_i(Z) = GW^{-gs}_i(Z) for i >= 4. Statements two and three were shown previously by Krannich and Kupers by geometric methods. The proofs compare the exact sequences for the genuine quadratic and genuine symmetric structures: for degree 2 one uses that GW^{-gq}_2(Z) -> L^{-gq}_2(Z) = L^{gq}_0(Z) = Z is injective with finite cokernel; for degree 1 that L^{-gq}_2(Z) -> L^{-gs}_2(Z) is the inclusion of the multiples of 8, that pi_1 of K(Z;Q^{gq}_-)_{hC_2} = Z/4 and that L^{-gq}_1(Z) = L^{-q}_1(Z) = 0; and for degree 3 that L^{-gq}_3(Z) = L^{gq}_1(Z) = 0 and L^{-gq}_4(Z) = L^{-gs}_4(Z) = L^{gs}_2(Z) = 0, so that the map from pi_3 of the homotopy orbits to GW^{-gs}_3(Z) = Z/48 is injective with cokernel L^{-gs}_3(Z) = Z/2, whence Z/24.
items.locator: Theorem 3.2.13 with its proof, p. 60; statements ii) and iii) are attributed to [KK21]

items.name: What the same methods give for a general number ring
items.statement: For the ring of integers O in a number field F, Proposition 3.1.11 and Corollary 1.3.15 make GW^s_{cl}(O;epsilon) -> GW^s_{cl}(O[1/2];epsilon) a 2-local equivalence in degrees >= 1, so that in principle the 2-local Grothendieck-Witt groups of O can be computed from the results of [KRO20]. The p-local homotopy for odd p is controlled by the isomorphisms GW^s_{cl,n}(O;epsilon)[1/2] = K_n(O;epsilon)[1/2]^{C_2} (+) L^s_n(O;epsilon)[1/2], where Lemma 3.2.4 determines the C_2-action on the 2-inverted K-groups; and by Corollary 2.3.2 the 2-inverted L-groups are non-zero only in degrees divisible by 4, where they are free modules over the 2-inverted integers of rank the number of real embeddings of F.
items.locator: Remark 3.2.14, pp. 60-61; the L-group rank is [MH73, Chapter IV.4]
items.note: The paper stops here: it says what is in principle computable rather than doing it, which is exactly the gap recorded for a general number ring.
